conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: Most common causative organism in UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: E. coli (gram-negative, ascending bowel flora)

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What does nitrites on urine dipstick indicate?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Gram-negative bacterial infection (convert nitrates to nitrites)

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What does leucocytes alone on dipstick (no nitrites) mean?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Do NOT treat as UTI — leucocytes alone = inflammation, not necessarily infection

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: First-line antibiotic for simple LUTI in women?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Trimethoprim 200mg BD × 3 days OR nitrofurantoin 100mg MR × 3 days

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: Why is nitrofurantoin avoided if eGFR <45?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Inadequate urinary concentration → ineffective, potentially toxic

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: Why is trimethoprim contraindicated in 1st trimester pregnancy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Folate antagonist → neural tube defects (spina bifida)

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: How long should UTI be treated in pregnancy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: 7 days (regardless of trimester)

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What should be treated in ALL pregnant women (even asymptomatic bacteriuria)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy increases risk of pyelonephritis + preterm labour

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: Pyelonephritis presentation?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Fever + loin pain + renal angle tenderness + nausea/vomiting + systemic upset

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What organism causes struvite stones via UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Proteus mirabilis (urease-producing → alkaline urine → staghorn calculi)

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What organisms most commonly cause UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: E. coli (~80%), Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young sexually active women, 2nd most common), Klebsiella, Proteus mirabilis (urease producer — alkaline urine, struvite stones), Enterococcus faecalis (catheter-associated).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the NICE definition of lower UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Symptoms of urinary frequency, dysuria, urgency, suprapubic pain without systemic features. LOWER = bladder/urethra. UPPER = kidneys (pyelonephritis) — fever, loin pain, systemic illness.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the clinical presentation of pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Fever >38°C, rigors, loin pain/tenderness (renal angle tenderness), nausea/vomiting, plus lower UTI symptoms (dysuria, frequency). Sepsis can develop — requires IV antibiotics.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is a catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: UTI in a patient with a urinary catheter — most common hospital-acquired infection. Organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus. Prevention: avoid unnecessary catheterisation, aseptic technique, remove early, closed drainage system.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What are the risk factors for UTI in women?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Sexual activity (mechanical inoculation), pregnancy (ureteric dilation + immunosuppression), menopause (loss of oestrogenic protection, vaginal atrophy), diabetes, urinary catheter, structural abnormalities (vesicoureteric reflux, obstruction).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is recurrent UTI and how is it defined?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Recurrent UTI: ≥2 infections in 6 months, or ≥3 in 12 months. May be relapse (same organism) or reinfection (different organism/new infection). Requires investigation (USS KUB, cystoscopy in appropriate patients) to exclude structural abnormality.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is asymptomatic bacteriuria and when should it be treated?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Bacteriuria without symptoms — usually NOT treated (increases antibiotic resistance, side effects). Treat in: pregnancy (risk of pyelonephritis/preterm labour), before urological procedures (risk of sepsis), kidney transplant recipients (first 3 months).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What are the symptoms of urethritis vs cystitis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Urethritis: dysuria + urethral discharge, sexually acquired (Chlamydia, gonorrhoea) — MSU often negative. Cystitis: dysuria + frequency + urgency + suprapubic pain — MSU positive. Key distinction: discharge = STI screen, not UTI antibiotics.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the NICE-recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated lower UTI in women?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg MR BD (or 50 mg QDS) for 3 days first-line; trimethoprim 200 mg BD for 3 days where local resistance is low. (3-day course for non-pregnant women; 7 days for pregnancy/complicated UTI/men.) Avoid nitrofurantoin if eGFR <45.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What antibiotics are recommended for pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD 7–14 days (first-line if not hospitalised). IV gentamicin/cefuroxime if hospitalised/septic. Co-amoxiclav alternative if sensitivities confirmed. Blood cultures before antibiotics if systemically unwell.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the appropriate management of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Treat regardless of symptoms — risk of ascending infection (30% develop pyelonephritis if untreated), preterm labour, low birth weight. Screen with MSU at booking. Treat with oral antibiotics (nitrofurantoin safe in 1st/2nd trimester; amoxicillin if sensitive).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is a complicated UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: UTI with structural abnormality, functional abnormality, immunosuppression, obstruction, or in a special host (male, pregnant, diabetic, transplant recipient, catheterised). Requires longer antibiotic courses and investigation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and its significance?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Abnormal retrograde urine flow from bladder to ureter/kidney during voiding. Can cause recurrent UTIs and reflux nephropathy (renal scarring) → hypertension and CKD. Children with UTI should be investigated for VUR (NICE guidelines).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What investigations are recommended after first UTI in a child?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: NICE: infant <6 months with a first UTI → renal USS (within 6 weeks if it responds well to treatment; during the acute infection only if atypical or recurrent). 6 months–3 years: USS if atypical or recurrent. >3 years: USS if recurrent or atypical. DMSA (4–6 months later) for scarring in atypical/recurrent UTI; MCUG only if high-grade VUR suspected.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is emphysematous pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Severe necrotising infection of renal parenchyma with gas-forming organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella) — almost exclusively in diabetics. CT shows gas in renal parenchyma. High mortality (20–40%). Requires IV antibiotics + urgent drainage (nephrostomy) ± nephrectomy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is a perinephric abscess and its management?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Collection of pus in the perinephric space (between kidney and Gerota's fascia). Usually from ascending UTI or haematogenous spread. CT diagnosis. Management: IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage (nephrostomy) ± surgical drainage.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is renal abscess (intrarenal abscess) and how does it develop?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Collection within renal parenchyma. Usually ascending UTI (E. coli in diabetics/obstructed kidney) or haematogenous (Staph aureus — e.g. from skin infection). CT confirms. IV antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage. Small abscesses may resolve with antibiotics alone.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the treatment of UTI in men?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: UTI in men is always 'complicated' — assume prostatitis component. Treat with ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim for 7–14 days (longer courses than women). Investigate: MSU, USS KUB, PSA (after infection resolves). Consider prostate disease in older men.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: How does diabetes increase UTI risk?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Glucosuria provides bacterial substrate, impaired neutrophil function, bladder dysfunction (neurogenic bladder — incomplete emptying), immunosuppression. Higher risk of complicated infections (emphysematous pyelonephritis, renal abscess, fungal UTI).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What non-antibiotic measures reduce UTI recurrence in women?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Increased fluid intake, post-coital voiding, front-to-back wiping, avoid bubble bath/feminine hygiene products. Topical oestrogen (postmenopausal). D-mannose (binds E. coli type 1 pili). Cranberry products (modest evidence). Prophylactic trimethoprim if ≥3/year.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What urine culture result is diagnostic of UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: MSU: ≥105 colony forming units (CFU)/mL of a single organism with pyuria (>10 WBC/HPF). Lower counts (103–104 CFU/mL) may be significant in symptomatic patients, males, catheter samples. Polymicrobial growth usually suggests contamination.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What prophylactic antibiotic regime is used for recurrent UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Once-daily low-dose trimethoprim 100 mg or nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg at night for 6 months. OR post-coital single dose. Reviewed regularly — promotes resistance long-term. Alternative: self-start therapy (patient-initiated course at first symptoms).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the significance of nitrite on urine dipstick?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Nitrites = presence of Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella etc.) converting urinary nitrates to nitrites. Highly specific for UTI (~90%). Sensitivity ~50% (false negatives if non-nitrite-producing organisms, dilute urine, rapid transit). Leucocyte esterase = WBC (pyuria).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the management of a renal transplant patient with UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Treat aggressively — UTI in transplant recipient can rapidly lead to pyelonephritis of the transplanted kidney and rejection. Use transplant-safe antibiotics (avoid nephrotoxic agents, check interactions with immunosuppressants). Asymptomatic bacteriuria treated for first 3–6 months post-transplant.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is recurrent cystitis in postmenopausal women and its treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Oestrogen deficiency → vaginal atrophy, loss of lactobacilli, alkaline vaginal pH → colonisation by uropathogens. Treatment: topical oestrogen (vaginal cream/pessary) — reduces recurrence rate by 60–70%. Systemic HRT has no proven benefit for UTI prevention.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: When should a urological investigation be organised for UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Men (first UTI), recurrent UTI (≥2 in 6 months or ≥3 in 12 months), upper UTI (pyelonephritis), suspected structural abnormality, failure to respond to antibiotics, haematuria (persistent after treatment — exclude malignancy), children (per NICE guidance).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is XGP (xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Rare chronic destructive renal infection — usually Proteus/E. coli in obstructed kidney. Foamy lipid-laden macrophages ('foam cells'). Mimics renal carcinoma on imaging. Usually requires nephrectomy (destroyed kidney). Pathognomonic: staghorn calculus + non-functioning kidney on isotope scan.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What is the difference between upper and lower UTI based on clinical features?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Lower UTI (cystitis): dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain — NO systemic features. Upper UTI (pyelonephritis): all lower UTI symptoms PLUS fever ≥38°C, rigors, loin pain, renal angle tenderness, nausea/vomiting, raised CRP/WBC — systemic illness requiring IV antibiotics if severe.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: What fungal organism can cause UTI, particularly in catheterised and diabetic patients?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: Candida species (usually C. albicans). Risk factors: broad-spectrum antibiotics, urinary catheter, diabetes, immunosuppression. Treatment: fluconazole if symptomatic or immunocompromised/renal transplant. Asymptomatic candiduria in non-immunocompromised: remove catheter/change antibiotics, usually clears without antifungals.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the FOUR key management points for UTI?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.back: 1) Uncomplicated female: trimethoprim/nitrofurantoin 7 days. 2) Pyelonephritis: ciprofloxacin 7–14 days (IV if septic). 3) Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat ONLY in pregnancy, pre-urological procedure, transplant. 4) Recurrent UTI in women: non-antibiotic measures first; prophylaxis if ≥3/year.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What is pyelonephritis, and what defines it?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Bacterial infection of the renal pelvis and parenchyma — the upper-tract UTI. Defined by the systemic triad on top of lower-UTI symptoms — that triad is what separates it from cystitis and signals the sepsis/scarring risk.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: Contrast lower UTI (cystitis) and upper UTI (pyelonephritis) by symptoms.
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Lower UTI (cystitis): dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain — local symptoms only. Upper UTI (pyelonephritis): lower-UTI symptoms + fever + loin pain + nausea/vomiting — systemic upset with sepsis risk.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What are the risk factors for pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Female sex; structural urological abnormalities; vesico-ureteric reflux (VUR) — especially children; diabetes mellitus; obstruction/stasis — stones, catheter, pregnancy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What is the key paediatric risk factor for pyelonephritis?
What are the causative organisms of pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: E. coli — commonest (gut flora ascending); Klebsiella pneumoniae; Enterococcus; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Staphylococcus saprophyticus; Candida albicans (fungal).

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What is the defining triad of pyelonephritis (on top of lower-UTI symptoms)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: 1. Fever. 2. Loin / back pain (uni- or bilateral). 3. Nausea / vomiting.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What are the additional clinical features of pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Systemic illness, loss of appetite, haematuria; renal angle (costovertebral) tenderness on examination.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What investigations are used in pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Urine dipstick — nitrites, leucocytes, blood. MSU (midstream urine) — microscopy, culture and sensitivity; collect before starting antibiotics. Bloods — raised WCC, raised CRP. Imaging (USS or CT) — exclude renal stones, abscess, or other pathology.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: Why must the MSU be collected before starting antibiotics?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: So the sample gives an accurate microscopy, culture and sensitivity result before antibiotics affect it.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What is the community management of pyelonephritis (7–10 days)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Cefalexin — first choice; co-amoxiclav or trimethoprim — if sensitivities available; ciprofloxacin — caution: tendon damage + lowers seizure threshold.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What is the first-choice antibiotic for community-managed pyelonephritis, and for how long?
What cautions apply to ciprofloxacin in pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Tendon damage + lowers the seizure threshold.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: How is a septic patient with pyelonephritis managed (Sepsis Six)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Admit. 3 tests: lactate, blood cultures, urine output. 3 treatments: O₂ to 94–98% (88–92% in COPD), IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluids.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: If a patient with pyelonephritis is not responding or has severe symptoms, what two things should you think of?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: 1. Renal abscess — needs drainage. 2. Obstructing stone — an infected + obstructed kidney needs urgent decompression, not just antibiotics.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: Why does an infected, obstructed kidney need urgent decompression rather than just antibiotics?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: An infected + obstructed kidney is a urological emergency — antibiotics alone won't clear it; it needs urgent decompression.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What is chronic pyelonephritis, and what does it lead to?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Recurrent kidney infections → scarring of the renal parenchyma → chronic kidney disease → end-stage renal failure.

conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.front: What is a DMSA scan, and how is it used in pyelonephritis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis.back: Radiolabelled DMSA accumulates in healthy kidney tissue. Areas that don't take it up on gamma-camera imaging indicate scarring/damage — used to assess renal damage in recurrent pyelonephritis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the core job when assessing a scrotal lump, and which two presentations are can't-miss?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: It's a differential-diagnosis problem: place the lump in the right box. One box (cancer) and one acute presentation (torsion) are can't-miss. Three questions resolve most lumps.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: Question 1 of the scrotal lump examination: 'Can you get above it?'
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: No → inguinoscrotal hernia (abdominal origin). Yes → scrotal lump.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: Question 2 of the scrotal lump examination: 'Separate from testis?'
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Separate → epididymal cyst / varicocele. Part of testis → hydrocele or tumour.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: Question 3 of the scrotal lump examination: 'Does it transilluminate?'
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Yes → cystic/benign. No → solid → ? cancer.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the discriminating features of a hydrocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Surrounds the testis, soft, fluctuant; transilluminates YES; key clue — testis palpable within it; may be large.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the discriminating features of an epididymal cyst?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Above + separate from testis (epididymal head); transilluminates YES (if large); key clue — smooth, fluctuant, often multiple, middle-aged men.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the discriminating features of a varicocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: 'Bag of worms,' separate from testis; does NOT transilluminate; key clue — dragging sensation; disappears on lying flat.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the discriminating features of a testicular tumour?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Part of testis, hard, irregular; does NOT transilluminate; key clue — does not transilluminate → 2WW referral.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the discriminating features of epididymo-orchitis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Tender, swollen, painful; does NOT transilluminate; key clue — acute, ± fever, dysuria.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the discriminating features of testicular torsion as a scrotal lump?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Acute severe pain, high-riding; does NOT transilluminate; key clue — surgical emergency.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the discriminating features of an inguinal hernia?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Can't get above it, ± bowel sounds; does NOT transilluminate; key clue — reducible, cough impulse.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is a hydrocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: A collection of fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Painless, soft scrotal swelling — testis palpable within it. Transilluminates.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the causes of a simple (adult) hydrocele, and what must always be excluded?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Imbalance of fluid secretion/absorption; idiopathic or secondary (trauma, infection, tumour). Always exclude underlying testicular pathology with USS in new adult hydroceles.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is a communicating (infant) hydrocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: A patent processus vaginalis — peritoneal fluid tracks into the scrotum. Often resolves spontaneously.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the management of a hydrocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Idiopathic → reassure/conservative; surgery if large/symptomatic.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is a varicocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Abnormal dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus — 'bag of worms,' dragging sensation, may disappear on lying flat.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: Why are varicoceles far more common on the left?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle (the right drains directly into the IVC), making the left more prone to congestion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the red flag for a varicocele, and why?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: A varicocele that does NOT disappear on lying down, or a right-sided varicocele → suspect a retroperitoneal tumour obstructing venous drainage → urgent USS to exclude renal malignancy (same left-renal-vein anatomy as the RCC varicocele sign).

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the key complication of a varicocele, and its mechanism?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: A varicocele is a reversible cause of male infertility — it raises scrotal temperature, impairing spermatogenesis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the management of a varicocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Conservative if uncomplicated; surgery or embolisation for pain, testicular atrophy, or infertility.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is an epididymal cyst / spermatocele?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: A fluid-filled sac at the head of the epididymis. If it contains sperm = spermatocele (management identical). Very common (~30% of men), usually asymptomatic.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the features of an epididymal cyst?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Smooth, fluctuant, above and separate from the testis, transilluminates; often multiple; classically middle-aged men; no malignancy association.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the management of an epididymal cyst?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Rarely needs treatment; surgery only if large/painful — avoid in younger men (infertility and chronic pain risk).

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is epididymo-orchitis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Inflammation of the epididymis ± testis. Painful, swollen, tender ± fever, dysuria, urethral discharge.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What are the causative organisms of epididymo-orchitis by age?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: <35 / sexually active: STI — Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea (STI testing + contact tracing). >35 / older: enteric organisms — E. coli (UTI-type pathology).

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What must always be considered in a young man with an acute painful scrotum?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: Must distinguish from torsion — if in doubt in a young man with an acute painful scrotum, treat as torsion (surgical exploration) until proven otherwise.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the role of scrotal ultrasound in scrotal lumps?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: The key investigation for any uncertain lump; differentiates fluid (benign) from solid (tumour); Doppler assesses varicocele flow and torsion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: What is the role of transillumination as an investigation?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: A bedside test (fluid vs solid).

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: Which tumour markers are checked, and when?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: AFP, βHCG, LDH — if the lump is solid or suspicious.

conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.front: When are urine + STI swabs indicated?
conditions__UROLOGY__Scrotal Lumps.back: If epididymo-orchitis is suspected.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is testicular torsion, and why is it an emergency?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Twisting of the spermatic cord with rotation of the testicle. A urological emergency — delay causes ischaemia and necrosis, leading to sub-fertility or infertility. Typical patient: a teenage boy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the surgical time window for testicular torsion, and what does imaging's role mean?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Surgery within 6 hours of pain onset → >90% testicular salvage. Imaging must NEVER delay surgery — if torsion is clinically suspected, the patient goes to theatre.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: Contrast the onset and typical age of testicular torsion vs epididymo-orchitis.
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Torsion: sudden, acute onset; teenage boy (peak). Epididymo-orchitis: more gradual onset; <35 STI-related / >35 enteric.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: Contrast the pain in testicular torsion vs epididymo-orchitis.
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Torsion: severe ± abdominal pain/vomiting. Epididymo-orchitis: tender ± fever/dysuria.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the cremasteric reflex in torsion vs epididymo-orchitis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Torsion: absent. Epididymo-orchitis: present.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is Prehn's sign, and how does it differ in torsion vs epididymo-orchitis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Torsion: negative — elevation does NOT relieve pain. Epididymo-orchitis: positive — elevation relieves pain.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the immediate action for torsion vs epididymo-orchitis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Torsion: theatre NOW. Epididymo-orchitis: antibiotics.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the golden rule when torsion vs epididymo-orchitis is uncertain?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: If there is ANY doubt — treat as torsion. Explore surgically; do not wait.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the ischaemia sequence in testicular torsion?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: The cord twists → veins occlude first (low pressure) → congestion + swelling → then arterial inflow is cut off → ischaemia → infarction.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the bell-clapper deformity, and why does it matter?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: The testis is not fixed to the tunica vaginalis → hangs horizontally and rotates freely like a bell clapper. It is the predisposing anatomy — and explains why bilateral fixation is done (the contralateral side has the same deformity).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What are the clinical features of testicular torsion?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Acute, rapid-onset unilateral testicular pain ± abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting. Often triggered by activity/sport — ask what the patient was doing at onset. A history of intermittent self-resolving episodes suggests intermittent torsion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: Why must you examine the testes in a boy presenting with abdominal pain? (classic exam trap)
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Abdominal pain may be the only symptom in boys — always examine the testes in a boy presenting with abdominal pain. Missing this is a classic exam trap (torsion can present without scrotal symptoms).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What are the key examination findings in testicular torsion?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Cremasteric reflex absent — stroking the inner thigh fails to elevate the testis. High-riding, horizontally lying testis — swollen, exquisitely tender. Negative Prehn's sign — elevating the testis does not relieve pain.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: How is testicular torsion diagnosed, and what is the role of imaging?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Diagnosis is clinical. If torsion is suspected, get immediate senior urology input and proceed to theatre. Negative imaging never overrides clinical suspicion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the role of Doppler ultrasound in suspected torsion?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Doppler USS can show absent/reduced testicular blood flow — but only if it does NOT delay theatre. A normal Doppler scan does NOT exclude torsion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the immediate management of suspected testicular torsion?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: NBM (nil by mouth), analgesia, urgent urology referral.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What is the definitive step in torsion management?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Urgent scrotal exploration — the definitive step; do not delay.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: At surgery, how is a viable testis managed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Detorsion + bilateral orchidopexy (fix both).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: At surgery, how is a non-viable testis managed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Orchidectomy + fix contralateral side.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: Why is bilateral fixation always performed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: The bell-clapper deformity is bilateral — the contralateral testis has the same anatomy and is at equal risk. Always fix both sides at surgery (even if one side is removed).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.front: What are the testicular salvage rates by time from onset?
How should recurrent self-resolving episodes of testicular pain be managed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Torsion.back: Intermittent torsion — recurrent self-resolving episodes still need elective bilateral fixation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is urinary incontinence, and what is the decisive fork in approaching it?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Involuntary leakage of urine. The decisive fork = which type — each has a distinct mechanism, a distinct history, and type-specific management.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What are the four types of urinary incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Stress, urge (OAB), mixed, and overflow.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the mechanism and characteristic history of stress incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Mechanism: weak pelvic floor / sphincter. History that gives it away: leakage on laughing, coughing, sneezing, exertion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the mechanism and characteristic history of urge incontinence (OAB)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Mechanism: detrusor overactivity. History that gives it away: sudden urge with loss of control on the way to the toilet.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is mixed incontinence, and what is the key management principle?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Mechanism: urge + stress combined. History: both — identify which dominates and treat that first.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the mechanism and characteristic history of overflow incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Mechanism: chronic retention from outflow obstruction. History that gives it away: leakage without the urge to pass urine.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What are the risk factors for stress incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Childbirth/vaginal delivery, age, obesity, menopause, pelvic surgery.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: How is the clinical picture of urge incontinence summarised?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Detrusor overactivity → sudden urgency, frequency, nocturia — the 'gotta go' picture, where urgency is the dominant feature.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What are the causes of overflow incontinence ('retention in disguise')?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Chronic retention → leakage without urge. Causes: BPH, anticholinergic drugs, fibroids, pelvic tumours, neurological (MS, diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord injury).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the key history discriminator between stress and urge incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Cough/sneeze leak (stress) vs sudden urge with loss of control on the way to the toilet (urge). Also assess caffeine, alcohol, fluid intake, weight.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is assessed on examination in urinary incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Ask the patient to cough and observe for leakage; assess pelvic muscle strength by asking her to squeeze against examining fingers → modified Oxford grading system.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is a bladder diary, and how long should it be kept?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Track fluid intake and voiding/incontinence episodes for ≥3 days, including a mix of work and leisure days.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What does a urine dipstick assess in urinary incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Assess for infection, microscopic haematuria, and other pathology.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: When are urodynamic studies used?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Specialist test — used if the diagnosis is unclear or before surgery.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the stepwise management of stress incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: 1. Lifestyle — reduce caffeine/alcohol, optimise fluid intake, weight loss. 2. Pelvic floor exercises — supervised, ≥3 months before considering surgery (first-line). 3. Duloxetine — SNRI, second-line if surgery declined or unsuitable. 4. Surgery — tension-free vaginal tape / colposuspension; artificial urinary sphincter if neurological cause.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the first-line treatment for stress incontinence, and how long is it trialled?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Supervised pelvic floor exercises for ≥3 months before considering surgery.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the role of duloxetine in stress incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: An SNRI — second-line if surgery is declined or unsuitable.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What surgical options are used for stress incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Tension-free vaginal tape / colposuspension; artificial urinary sphincter if there is a neurological cause.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the stepwise management of urge incontinence / OAB?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: 1. Bladder retraining — gradually increase time between voiding, ≥6 weeks (first-line). 2. Anticholinergics — oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin. 3. Mirabegron — β-3 agonist, alternative with less anticholinergic burden. 4. Invasive (refractory) — botulinum toxin A, sacral nerve stimulation, augmentation cystoplasty, urinary diversion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the first-line treatment for urge incontinence / OAB, and its duration?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Bladder retraining — gradually increase the time between voiding, over ≥6 weeks.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: Which anticholinergics are used for urge incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is mirabegron, and what is its advantage in urge incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: A β-3 agonist — an alternative with less anticholinergic burden.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What are the invasive/refractory options for urge incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Botulinum toxin A; sacral nerve stimulation; augmentation cystoplasty; urinary diversion.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What are the side effects of anticholinergics used for OAB?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Dry mouth, dry eyes, constipation; urinary retention, postural hypotension; cognitive decline / worsening dementia — a major concern in older patients. Avoid oxybutynin in the frail elderly.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: Why should oxybutynin be avoided in the frail elderly?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Because of its anticholinergic side effects — particularly cognitive decline / worsening dementia (a significant anticholinergic burden).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the mirabegron caution? (high-yield)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: As a β-3 agonist it stimulates the sympathetic NS → raises BP. Contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension — risk of hypertensive crisis, TIA, stroke. Monitor BP.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.front: What is the management principle for overflow incontinence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Incontinenc.back: Treat the underlying cause — this is really a retention problem in disguise. Relieve the outflow obstruction (treat BPH, catheterise), stop causative drugs (anticholinergics), manage the neurological condition.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What is urinary retention, and what is the decisive fork?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Retention = inability to pass urine. The decisive fork = acute vs chronic — they feel completely different and carry different dangers.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: Contrast acute (AUR) and chronic (CUR) urinary retention by onset and pain.
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Acute (AUR): sudden onset; painful — distressing inability to void. Chronic (CUR): long-standing onset; painless — bladder desensitised by chronic distension.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: Contrast acute and chronic urinary retention by volumes and key danger.
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Acute (AUR): moderate volumes; key danger is acute distress + underlying cause. Chronic (CUR): can be very large volumes with minimal discomfort; key danger is high-pressure retention → hydronephrosis → AKI.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What are the obstructive causes of urinary retention (the commonest)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: BPH — most common cause in men; urethral stricture, prostate cancer; in women — pelvic prolapse (cystocele, rectocele, uterine) or pelvic mass (fibroids); constipation — compresses the urethra.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What are the non-obstructive ('other') causes of urinary retention?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Infective — UTI causes urethral sphincter closure (esp. in BPH); neurological — MS, peripheral neuropathy, spinal cord injury; drugs — antimuscarinics, opioids, spinal/epidural anaesthesia; post-operative — pain, constipation, infection, anaesthetic agents.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What is the red flag to never miss in urinary retention?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Cauda equina syndrome: urinary retention + saddle anaesthesia + back pain → emergency MRI. Do not miss.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: How does acute urinary retention present?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Sensation of needing to void but unable to micturate; little/no urine passed; suprapubic pain; palpable distended bladder.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What is the management sequence for acute urinary retention?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: 1. Urethral catheterisation — immediate relief (drain the bladder). 2. Investigations — bladder scan (volume), urine dip + MSU, U&Es (renal function). 3. Treat underlying cause, then TWOC (trial without catheter) when appropriate.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What is a TWOC, and when is the catheter removed in a patient with no renal impairment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: TWOC = trial without catheter. If no renal impairment, remove the catheter after treating the cause.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: How is TWOC managed in men with a large prostate / chronic LUTS?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Start tamsulosin (α-1 antagonist); do the TWOC >72 hours after starting (it relaxes the bladder neck → improves voiding success).

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What are the possible outcomes of a TWOC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Voids successfully with minimal residual → TWOC successful. Re-enters retention → re-catheterise; repeated failures → long-term catheter until definitive treatment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: How does chronic urinary retention present?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Painless, long-standing retention with large residual volumes. The bladder is desensitised — patients may pass small amounts but still retain significant volumes. Often presents as overflow incontinence (constant dribble).

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What is high-pressure chronic retention (HPCR), and what does it lead to?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: High intra-vesical pressure overcomes the bladder/ureter anti-reflux mechanism → urine backs up → hydroureter + hydronephrosis → AKI.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: When should you suspect high-pressure chronic retention, and how is it confirmed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Suspect HPCR if: >1000 mL drained on catheterisation, bilateral hydronephrosis, or unexplained AKI → USS to confirm.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What is the management of chronic urinary retention?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: Catheterise to decompress; treat the underlying cause; urology referral.

conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.front: What is post-obstructive diuresis, and what are its risks?
conditions__UROLOGY__Acute & Chronic Uri.back: After relieving large-volume retention, the kidneys produce massive urine volumes. Risk: dehydration + electrolyte loss. Monitor urine output + U&Es; replace fluids. Greater risk with chronic/HPCR than simple AUR.
Rapid bladder emptying → mucosal bleeding; usually self-limiting.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: Most common type of renal stone?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Calcium oxalate/phosphate (80%)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: Which stone type is radiolucent on plain X-ray?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Uric acid stones — CT still shows them

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What organism causes struvite staghorn calculi?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Proteus mirabilis (urease-producing)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: Gold standard investigation for renal stones?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Non-contrast CT KUB (kidneys, ureters, bladder)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: First-line analgesia for renal colic?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: IM diclofenac (NSAID) + antiemetic

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: When is urgent decompression needed for renal stones?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Obstruction + infection (obstructive pyelonephritis) — nephrostomy or ureteric stent URGENTLY

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: ESWL — what is it and when is it used?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy — for renal stones <2cm

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: Ureteroscopy + laser lithotripsy — when is it used?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: For ureteric stones

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: PCNL — what is it?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy — for large renal stones >2cm / staghorn calculi

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: How do thiazide diuretics prevent calcium stones?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: ↑distal tubular Ca²⁺ reabsorption → ↓urinary calcium excretion

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What are the four main types of renal stones and their relative frequencies?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Calcium oxalate/phosphate (~80% most common), struvite/magnesium ammonium phosphate (~10–15% — infection stones), uric acid (~5–10%), cystine (<1% — hereditary).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the classic presentation of renal colic?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Severe loin-to-groin pain (colicky, waves, patient cannot keep still), haematuria (micro or macro), nausea/vomiting. Pain follows ureter: loin → iliac fossa → groin/testicle/labia.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the first-line imaging for suspected renal colic?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Non-contrast CT KUB (kidneys, ureters, bladder) — gold standard. Detects >95% of stones, identifies complications. KUB X-ray (calcium stones radiopaque), USS (limited for ureteric stones). CT preferred in most adults.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What are the risk factors for calcium oxalate stones?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Hypercalciuria (hyperparathyroidism, vit D excess), hyperoxaluria (Crohn's, short bowel — increased oxalate absorption), hypocitraturia (low citrate — key inhibitor), low fluid intake, dehydration.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the most important modifiable risk factor for renal stone formation?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Inadequate fluid intake (concentrated urine promotes crystallisation). Target urine output >2 L/day. Advice: drink enough to keep urine pale yellow.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What type of stone is associated with Proteus mirabilis infection?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones — urease-producing bacteria (Proteus, Klebsiella) split urea → ammonia → alkaline urine → staghorn calculi. Associated with recurrent UTIs.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What are staghorn calculi and why are they significant?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Large stones filling the renal pelvis and calyces — usually struvite (infection). Can cause obstructive uropathy, recurrent infections, and renal failure. Require percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) for treatment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What type of stone is radiolucent on plain X-ray?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Uric acid stones — radiolucent (invisible on KUB). Seen on CT. Associated with low urine pH, gout, metabolic syndrome. Treatment: alkalinise urine (potassium citrate) + allopurinol for gout.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the management of acute renal colic?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Analgesia: NSAIDs first-line (diclofenac/ketorolac — reduce ureteric spasm), opioids if NSAIDs contraindicated. Alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) — medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteric stones ≤10 mm. IV fluids, antiemetics.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What stone size is likely to pass spontaneously?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: <5 mm: ~90% pass spontaneously. 5–10 mm: ~50% pass. >10 mm: unlikely to pass — intervention usually needed. Distal stones pass more easily than proximal ureteric stones.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What are the indications for urgent urological intervention in renal stone disease?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Obstructed infected kidney (sepsis) — emergency. Bilateral obstruction/obstruction of single kidney. Intractable pain/vomiting. Stone >10 mm unlikely to pass. Renal impairment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the treatment of choice for obstructed infected kidney (pyonephrosis)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Emergency decompression: nephrostomy tube or ureteric stent (JJ stent). Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Definitive stone treatment deferred until sepsis controlled. Delay = septicaemia and renal loss.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is ESWL and when is it used?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy — ultrasound shockwaves fragment stones. Used for stones <2 cm in renal pelvis or proximal ureter. Outpatient procedure. Contraindicated: pregnancy, aortic aneurysm, coagulopathy, pacemaker (relative).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is ureteroscopy (URS) and when is it preferred over ESWL?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Flexible/semi-rigid scope passed via urethra → bladder → ureter → stone. Laser lithotripsy (holmium) fragments stone. Preferred for distal ureteric stones, ESWL-resistant stones, radiolucent stones, and when anatomical access limits ESWL.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is PCNL and when is it used?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy — nephroscope inserted directly into renal pelvis percutaneously. Used for large renal stones (>2 cm), staghorn calculi, failed ESWL. Higher complication rate (bleeding, infection) but most effective for large stones.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What metabolic investigations should be performed after a first stone episode?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Serum calcium (hyperparathyroidism), urate (gout), renal function, urinalysis/urine culture. 24-hour urine (calcium, oxalate, urate, citrate, phosphate) if recurrent/bilateral/family history/metabolic risk. Stone analysis if retrieved.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the medical management to prevent recurrent calcium stones?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: High fluid intake (>2 L urine output/day), dietary calcium adequate (do NOT restrict — binds dietary oxalate in gut), reduce sodium and animal protein, thiazide diuretics (reduce urinary calcium), potassium citrate (increases citrate, alkalinises urine).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the link between hyperparathyroidism and renal stones?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Primary hyperparathyroidism → elevated PTH → hypercalcaemia + hypercalciuria → calcium stone formation. Stones are one of the classic presentations of primary HPT. Check serum calcium in all first-time stone formers.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is cystinuria and what stones does it cause?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Autosomal recessive defect in renal tubular transport of COAL (Cystine, Ornithine, Arginine, Lysine) → cystinuria → hexagonal cystine crystals on urine microscopy → cystine stones. Managed with high fluid intake, alkalinisation, D-penicillamine.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What blood tests may be abnormal in renal colic?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: FBC (WCC raised if infection), U&E (AKI if obstructed), calcium (hyperparathyroidism), urate (gout), CRP (sepsis). Urinalysis: haematuria (95%), leucocytes/nitrites if UTI, pH (low = uric acid; alkaline = struvite).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the Hounsfield unit (HU) and why does it matter in renal stone CT?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: HU measures stone density on CT. High density (>1000 HU) = calcium stones, hard, may resist ESWL. Low density (<500 HU) = uric acid/cystine — better response to ESWL. Guides treatment selection.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the role of alpha-blockers in ureteric stone management?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker): relaxes smooth muscle of distal ureter → increases spontaneous stone passage rate for stones ≤10 mm. Medical expulsive therapy — reduces need for intervention in smaller stones.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What urinary pH suggests uric acid stone formation?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Low urinary pH (<5.5) — uric acid is more soluble in alkaline urine. Treatment: potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine to pH 6–6.5. Uric acid stones can dissolve with alkalinisation (unlike calcium stones).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What complication arises from a JJ stent left in situ too long?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Stent encrustation (calcium deposits on stent material) → stone formation on the stent itself → difficult/impossible removal. All stents should be removed/exchanged within recommended time frames (usually 3–12 months depending on material).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is obstructive uropathy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Obstruction of urinary tract → back pressure → hydronephrosis → progressive renal damage. Causes by level: upper (stone, UPJ obstruction), mid-ureteral (stone, retroperitoneal fibrosis), bladder outflow (BPH, prostate cancer, urethral stricture). Unilateral vs bilateral.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the difference between nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Nephrolithiasis = discrete renal/ureteric stones. Nephrocalcinosis = diffuse calcium deposition in renal parenchyma — seen in medullary sponge kidney, hyperparathyroidism, renal tubular acidosis, hypercalcaemia. Nephrocalcinosis predisposes to recurrent stones.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is medullary sponge kidney and its stone risk?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Congenital malformation of medullary collecting ducts → dilated tubules → urinary stasis → calcium stone formation and nephrocalcinosis. Diagnosed on IVU (brush-like appearance). Usually benign; managed with high fluid intake.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What is the significance of haematuria in renal colic?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Haematuria (macro or micro) is present in ~95% of ureteric colic cases — blood from stone trauma to urothelium. HOWEVER: absence of haematuria does NOT exclude a stone. Must also exclude bladder/renal tract malignancy in appropriate patients.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: What are the complications of an untreated obstructing ureteric stone?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Hydronephrosis, hydroureter, pyelonephritis, pyonephrosis (pus in obstructed kidney — emergency), urosepsis, permanent renal damage/loss if obstruction prolonged, AKI (bilateral or single kidney).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the classic presentation, key investigation, and first-line analgesia for renal colic?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease.back: Classic: loin-to-groin colicky pain + haematuria. Key investigation: non-contrast CT KUB. First-line analgesia: IV/IM diclofenac (NSAID — reduces ureteric spasm). Urgent intervention if obstructed infected kidney (emergency decompression).

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: Symptoms of BPH: storage vs voiding?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Storage: urgency/frequency/nocturia. Voiding: hesitancy/weak stream/terminal dribbling/incomplete emptying.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the alpha-1 blocker used for BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Tamsulosin — relaxes smooth muscle in bladder neck

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: SE of tamsulosin?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Postural hypotension + retrograde ejaculation

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What does finasteride do?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: 5-alpha reductase inhibitor — blocks testosterone → DHT conversion → ↓prostate size. Takes 6 months.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is TURP syndrome?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Glycine absorption during TURP → dilutional hyponatraemia → confusion, visual changes

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: How is acute urinary retention managed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Emergency urethral catheterisation (check PSA before catheter)

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What does DRE show in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Smooth, symmetrical, soft, enlarged prostate with maintained central sulcus

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What does the IPSS score measure and what score indicates severe LUTS?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: International Prostate Symptom Score (0-35): mild 0-7, moderate 8-19, severe 20-35. Includes 7 symptom questions + 1 QoL question.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What urodynamic finding confirms bladder outlet obstruction in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: High detrusor pressure with low urinary flow rate (Pdet.Qmax >40 cmH2O with Qmax <10 mL/s). Pressure-flow studies are gold standard.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is a clinically significant post-void residual (PVR) volume?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: >150-200 mL is clinically significant. PVR >300 mL suggests chronic urinary retention. Measured by bladder ultrasound scan.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is overflow incontinence and how does it present?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Continuous dribbling of urine from an overdistended bladder. Occurs in chronic urinary retention — bladder pressure exceeds urethral resistance. Presents as constant dampness/dribbling.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: Define chronic urinary retention (CUR) and differentiate low vs high pressure.
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: CUR: chronic painless bladder distension with PVR >300 mL after voiding. Low pressure: no upper tract damage. High pressure: elevated intravesical pressure causing bilateral hydronephrosis and renal impairment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the indication for combination therapy (alpha blocker + 5-ARI) in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Prostate volume >30-40 mL with moderate-severe LUTS (IPSS ≥8) and PSA >1.4 ng/mL. MTOPS/CombAT trials showed combination superior for preventing progression.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the mechanism of tadalafil (PDE5 inhibitor) in LUTS/BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, increasing cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation in prostate, bladder neck, and urethra. Also approved for LUTS even without erectile dysfunction.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the mechanism of action of alpha-1 blockers in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Block alpha-1A adrenoceptors in prostate smooth muscle and bladder neck → relaxation → reduced urethral resistance → improved urinary flow. Onset within days.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What effect does finasteride have on PSA levels?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Finasteride (5-ARI) reduces PSA by ~50% after 6 months. To interpret PSA on finasteride, double the measured value. Failure to suppress PSA raises concern for prostate cancer.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the key difference between acute and chronic urinary retention?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Acute retention: sudden painful inability to void, requires emergency catheterisation. Chronic retention: painless, gradual, large PVR, may present with overflow incontinence or renal failure.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the most common complication of TURP?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Retrograde ejaculation occurs in ~65-90% of men post-TURP due to damage to bladder neck. Other complications: bleeding (5%), urethral stricture (5%), incontinence (<1%), TUR syndrome.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is TUR syndrome and what causes it?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Dilutional hyponatraemia from absorption of hypotonic irrigant (glycine) during TURP. Presents with confusion, hypertension, bradycardia. Risk increases with resection >1 hour. Treat with IV saline ± furosemide.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the indication for open simple prostatectomy (Millin's) for BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Prostate volume >80-100 mL, when TURP technically difficult; also indicated with bladder stones/diverticula requiring concurrent repair. Increasingly replaced by HoLEP.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is HoLEP and what is its advantage over TURP?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Holmium Laser Enucleation of the Prostate: enucleates entire adenoma using holmium laser. Size-independent, lower blood loss, shorter catheter time, equivalent functional outcomes to open prostatectomy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: How is a bladder scan (portable ultrasound) used in BPH management?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Non-invasive measurement of post-void residual volume. Used to diagnose urinary retention, monitor treatment response, guide decision for catheterisation. Rapid bedside tool.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the pathophysiological basis of BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Benign hyperplasia of periurethral transitional zone glands (not peripheral zone). Driven by DHT (dihydrotestosterone) from 5-alpha reductase conversion of testosterone. Causes static (mechanical) and dynamic (smooth muscle tone) obstruction.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What are the two main risk factors for BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Age (prevalence 50% at age 60, 90% at 85) and androgens (testosterone/DHT). Castrated men do not develop BPH. Obesity and metabolic syndrome also associated.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: How does BPH cause renal impairment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Chronic bladder outlet obstruction → high-pressure chronic retention → bilateral hydronephrosis → obstructive uropathy → post-renal acute kidney injury (elevated creatinine, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis on USS).

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the approach to haematuria workup in a patient with known BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: BPH alone rarely causes significant haematuria — must exclude bladder cancer and upper tract TCC. Requires flexible cystoscopy + upper tract imaging (CT urogram). Do not attribute haematuria to BPH without exclusion of malignancy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the standard catheter management after acute urinary retention?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Insert urethral catheter (or suprapubic if urethral route fails), allow slow decompression (clamp catheter if >500 mL drained rapidly to avoid haematuria). Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis. Keep catheter 24-48 hours then TWOC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is a trial without catheter (TWOC) and when is it performed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Removal of catheter to assess if patient can void spontaneously, usually 24-48 hours after acute retention (with alpha blocker started). Success rate ~50-60%. Failed TWOC → re-catheterise and consider surgical intervention.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What are contraindications to alpha-1 blockers?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Postural hypotension, concurrent PDE5 inhibitor use (risk of severe hypotension), first-dose hypotension (especially tamsulosin less so). Caution in planned cataract surgery (intraoperative floppy iris syndrome — IFIS).

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What are the sexual side effects of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Erectile dysfunction (~5%), decreased libido (~5%), ejaculatory dysfunction (~4%), gynaecomastia/breast tenderness (~2%). Effects may persist after discontinuation (post-finasteride syndrome).

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What are the criteria for watchful waiting in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Mild symptoms (IPSS <8), no complications (no retention, infection, stones, renal impairment), patient preference. Annual review with IPSS, flow rate, PVR. Lifestyle advice (fluid restriction, avoid caffeine/alcohol, timed voiding).

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the evidence for phytotherapy (saw palmetto) in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Serenoa repens (saw palmetto) — proposed 5-ARI and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Large RCTs (STEP, CAMUS trials) showed no significant benefit over placebo. Not recommended in UK guidelines but widely used.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax) and what value suggests obstruction?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Qmax measured by uroflowmetry (requires >150 mL void for accuracy). Normal Qmax >15 mL/s. <10 mL/s suggests significant outflow obstruction. 10-15 mL/s equivocal.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What does cystoscopy reveal in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Enlarged lateral lobes and median lobe causing bladder outlet obstruction, trabeculation (hypertrophied detrusor), cellules/diverticula, bladder stones. Used to exclude bladder cancer in haematuria workup.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What PSA level is associated with BPH vs prostate cancer concern?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: PSA 0-4 ng/mL generally normal; PSA can be elevated in BPH (typically <10 ng/mL). PSA density >0.15 ng/mL/cc, free:total PSA <15%, or rising PSA velocity >0.75 ng/mL/year raises cancer concern.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the mechanism of doxazosin vs tamsulosin in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Both are alpha-1 blockers. Doxazosin: non-selective alpha-1 blocker, more systemic hypotension, also used for hypertension. Tamsulosin: selective alpha-1A/D, more prostate-specific, less postural hypotension.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is alfuzosin and how does it differ from tamsulosin?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Alfuzosin: alpha-1 blocker with uroselectivity. Lower risk of ejaculatory dysfunction compared to tamsulosin. Once daily formulation. Similar efficacy. Less retrograde ejaculation — preferred when preserving ejaculation important.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is the differential diagnosis of LUTS in men?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: BPH, prostate cancer, urethral stricture, bladder overactivity (OAB), UTI, bladder cancer, neurogenic bladder (MS, Parkinson's, spinal cord injury), medications (anticholinergics, diuretics), diabetes insipidus.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: How do bladder stones form as a complication of BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Urinary stasis from incomplete bladder emptying (high PVR) → concentrated urine → crystallisation → bladder stone formation (usually struvite or calcium oxalate). Presents with haematuria, dysuria, interrupted stream, recurrent UTIs.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.front: What is post-obstructive diuresis and how is it managed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.back: Massive diuresis following relief of chronic urinary obstruction — due to osmotic diuresis, tubular dysfunction, and ANP release. Monitor urine output hourly; replace 50% of urine output with IV fluids to avoid dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: Most common cancer in men in the UK?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Prostate cancer

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: PSA false positive rate?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: 75% — most elevated PSAs are NOT cancer

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: Causes of raised PSA other than cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: BPH, prostatitis, UTI, recent ejaculation, vigorous exercise, DRE, catheterisation

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: DRE findings in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Hard, craggy, irregular, asymmetrical with loss of central sulcus

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: First-line investigation for suspected localised prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI)

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: Gleason score: what does 7 mean?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Intermediate-risk disease (3+4 is lower risk than 4+3)

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: Where do prostate cancer bone metastases appear on X-ray?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: SCLEROTIC (white/dense) — unlike lytic lesions of myeloma/RCC

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is GnRH agonist tumour flare?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Initial testosterone surge on starting GnRH agonist → need anti-androgen (bicalutamide) cover for 2–4 weeks

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What complication from spinal bone mets requires emergency treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) — most often thoracic. Urgent whole-spine MRI + high-dose dexamethasone + urgent radiotherapy (or surgery). (Cauda equina syndrome specifically refers to compression below the cord, L1/2 and lower.)

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is the Gleason grading system?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Microscopic grading of prostate cancer architecture; primary + secondary pattern (each 1-5) summed to give Gleason score 2-10; higher score = more aggressive

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What are the ISUP grade groups (1-5) and corresponding Gleason scores?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Group 1: Gleason ≤6 | Group 2: 3+4=7 | Group 3: 4+3=7 | Group 4: 4+4=8 | Group 5: 9-10

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What are the NICE criteria for active surveillance in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: PSA <10, Gleason ≤6 (ISUP grade 1), T1-T2a, ≤50% biopsy cores positive; PSA density <0.15; monitor with PSA every 3-6 months and repeat MRI/biopsy

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What are the main indications for radical prostatectomy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Localised (T1-T2) or locally advanced (T3a) prostate cancer with life expectancy >10 years; also selected T3b; performed open, laparoscopic or robotic-assisted

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) for prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: High-energy X-rays delivered to prostate over ~4-8 weeks; used for localised, locally advanced and palliative settings; often combined with ADT for high-risk disease

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is brachytherapy in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Radioactive seeds/wires inserted directly into prostate; LDR = permanent seeds (I-125); HDR = temporary high-dose iridium-192 wires; used for low-to-intermediate risk localised disease

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is the difference between HDR and LDR brachytherapy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: LDR (low-dose rate): permanent I-125 seeds, continuous low-dose radiation over months, suitable for low-risk; HDR (high-dose rate): temporary Ir-192, short high-dose fractions, often combined with EBRT for high-risk

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What are the main side effects of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Hot flushes, osteoporosis (fracture risk), gynaecomastia, loss of libido/erectile dysfunction, metabolic syndrome (insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, cardiovascular risk), fatigue, anaemia, cognitive effects

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: How does ADT cause osteoporosis and how is it prevented?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: ADT lowers testosterone → less aromatisation to oestrogen → increased osteoclastic bone resorption (high bone turnover) → osteoporosis. Prevent with calcium/Vit D, weight-bearing exercise, baseline DEXA; add denosumab or a bisphosphonate if high fracture risk.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is enzalutamide and its mechanism in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Second-generation anti-androgen; blocks androgen receptor (AR) binding, nuclear translocation and DNA binding; used in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and metastatic hormone-sensitive PCa

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is abiraterone and its mechanism?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: CYP17A1 inhibitor; blocks androgen synthesis in testes, adrenal glands and prostate tumour; must be given with prednisolone (to prevent mineralocorticoid excess); used in mCRPC and high-risk hormone-sensitive PCa

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is docetaxel's role in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: First chemotherapy shown to improve survival in mCRPC; microtubule stabiliser; 3-weekly cycles; side effects include neutropenia, peripheral neuropathy, alopecia; now also used upfront in high-volume metastatic hormone-sensitive PCa

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is PSMA PET scan and when is it used?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen PET-CT; detects PSMA-expressing PCa cells; used for staging high-risk disease, biochemical recurrence localisation, and selecting patients for Lu-177-PSMA therapy; more sensitive than conventional imaging

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What are the indications for a bone scan in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: PSA >10 ng/mL at diagnosis, Gleason ≥8, T3/T4 disease, bone pain, or PSA rising after treatment; Tc-99m bone scan shows areas of increased osteoblastic activity (sclerotic mets)

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is T staging in prostate cancer (key stages)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: T1: clinically inapparent; T2: confined within prostate (T2a ≤50% one lobe, T2b >50% one lobe, T2c both lobes); T3: extracapsular (T3a ECE, T3b SV invasion); T4: invades adjacent structures (bladder, rectum)

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is N and M staging in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: N0: no regional LN mets; N1: regional LN involved (obturator, iliac, presacral); M0: no distant mets; M1a: non-regional LN; M1b: bone; M1c: other distant sites (liver, lung)

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is biochemical recurrence (BCR) after radical prostatectomy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL confirmed on two consecutive measurements after RP; indicates residual/recurrent disease; management depends on PSA doubling time and PSMA PET staging

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is PSA doubling time and why is it clinically important?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Time for PSA to double; PSADT <3 months suggests aggressive metastatic disease with poor prognosis; PSADT >12 months more likely localised recurrence; guides decision on salvage radiotherapy vs systemic therapy

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: How is locally advanced prostate cancer (T3-T4, N0, M0) managed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Combination of EBRT + long-term ADT (2-3 years); or radical prostatectomy ± adjuvant radiotherapy; high-risk patients benefit from addition of docetaxel or abiraterone to ADT

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: How is metastatic prostate cancer initially managed?
