conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: ADT (GnRH agonist/antagonist or bilateral orchidectomy) + docetaxel or enzalutamide or abiraterone (triplet/doublet intensification); choice based on volume of disease, fitness, and comorbidities

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is the emergency management of prostate cancer spinal cord compression?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: High-dose dexamethasone 16mg immediately; urgent MRI spine; neurosurgical/orthopaedic review; radiotherapy within 24h if not surgical candidate; catheter if urinary retention; worst prognosis if already paraplegic at presentation

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: How does prostate cancer cause hypercalcaemia?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Osteolytic bone metastases (less common than osteoblastic) release calcium; PTHrP secretion (paraneoplastic); treat with IV fluids, bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) or denosumab; may cause confusion, constipation, polyuria

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is denosumab's role in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: RANK-L inhibitor; prevents osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; reduces skeletal-related events (fractures, SCC) in bone metastatic CRPC; also prevents bone loss from ADT; given SC monthly; risk of osteonecrosis of jaw

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is zoledronic acid's role in prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: IV bisphosphonate; inhibits osteoclasts; reduces skeletal-related events in mCRPC with bone mets; given 3-4 weekly; must check renal function and calcium; risk of osteonecrosis of jaw (ONJ)

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is the association between BRCA2 and prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: BRCA2 germline mutations increase PCa risk ~8-fold; associated with more aggressive disease, higher Gleason grade, earlier age of onset, higher metastatic rate and worse prognosis; screen family members

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What are PARP inhibitors in prostate cancer and which is approved?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: PARP inhibitors (e.g. olaparib, rucaparib) exploit synthetic lethality in homologous recombination-deficient (HRD) tumours; olaparib approved for mCRPC with BRCA1/2 or ATM mutations after progression on enzalutamide/abiraterone

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is the association between Lynch syndrome and prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Lynch syndrome (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 mutations) confers increased risk of prostate cancer; PCa in Lynch is often MSI-high; eligible for pembrolizumab (anti-PD1); accounts for ~2-5% of hereditary PCa

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What are the anatomical zones of the prostate and their significance?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Peripheral zone (70%): most cancers arise here, palpable on DRE; Central zone (25%): ejaculatory ducts pass through; Transitional zone (5%): site of BPH; Fibromuscular stroma anteriorly

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: Where does prostate cancer most commonly arise and why is this relevant?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: ~70-80% arise in peripheral zone → detectable on DRE and mpMRI; transitional zone cancers (~20%) often found incidentally in TURP chips; less likely to be palpable or cause early symptoms

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy and what are its implications?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Preservation of neurovascular bundles (NVB) running postero-laterally to prostate; reduces risk of erectile dysfunction; only appropriate if no extracapsular extension on that side; bilateral nerve-sparing gives best erectile outcomes

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.front: What is lutetium-177 PSMA therapy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.back: Radioligand therapy: Lu-177 conjugated to PSMA ligand → delivers beta radiation directly to PSMA-expressing PCa cells; approved for mCRPC after taxane and AR-pathway inhibitor; requires PSMA PET-positive scan; side effects: dry mouth, fatigue, cytopenias

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: Most common type of bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma (90%)

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: Most common presenting symptom of bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Painless visible haematuria

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: Most important risk factor for bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Smoking

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What occupational exposure increases bladder cancer risk?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Aromatic amines (dye industry, rubber industry)

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: 2WW referral criteria for bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Age >45 with visible haematuria (no UTI, or persisting after UTI treatment)

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is TURBT?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Transurethral resection of bladder tumour — for diagnosis and treatment of non-muscle-invasive disease

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What intravesical therapy is used for high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: BCG vaccine (stimulates immune response against tumour) or Mitomycin C

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: Definitive treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Radical cystectomy + neoadjuvant cisplatin + urinary diversion

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What organism causes SCC of the bladder?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Schistosoma haematobium (parasitic worm — endemic Middle East/Africa)

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the TNM staging for T0, Ta, T1, T2, T3, and T4 bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: T0: no tumour; Ta: non-invasive papillary; T1: invades lamina propria; T2: invades muscularis propria (T2a inner, T2b outer); T3: invades perivesical fat (T3a micro, T3b macro); T4: invades adjacent organs (T4a prostate/uterus/vagina, T4b pelvic/abdominal wall).

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the bladder and why is it important?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: CIS (Tis): flat, high-grade intraepithelial carcinoma, no papillary component. Appears red/velvety on cystoscopy. High malignant potential — 50% progress to muscle-invasive disease without treatment. Requires BCG intravesical immunotherapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: How are bladder tumours graded and what is the WHO 2004 classification?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: WHO 2004: papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential (PUNLMP), low-grade urothelial carcinoma, high-grade urothelial carcinoma. High-grade = aggressive, higher recurrence/progression risk. Replaces old G1/G2/G3 system.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What does cystoscopy show in bladder cancer and what are the biopsy findings?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Papillary (frond-like) or sessile lesions; CIS appears as flat erythematous patch. Biopsy confirms TCC histology, grade, and depth of invasion. Bimanual examination under anaesthesia determines fixation (T4b).

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the role of urine cytology in bladder cancer diagnosis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Detects shed malignant cells in urine. High sensitivity for high-grade TCC and CIS (70-90%), but low for low-grade tumours (<50%). Used as adjunct to cystoscopy. Positive cytology with normal cystoscopy → upper tract imaging.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: When is flexible vs rigid cystoscopy used in bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Flexible: diagnostic, outpatient, no anaesthesia, surveillance, initial haematuria investigation. Rigid: operative (TURBT), bimanual EUA, larger biopsies, cold cup biopsies of CIS. Rigid done under GA/spinal in theatre.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the haematuria clinic pathway for suspected bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: NICE NG12 2-week-wait: aged ≥45 with unexplained visible haematuria (without UTI, or persisting/recurring after UTI treatment), OR aged ≥60 with unexplained non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or a raised WCC. Clinic: flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram + urine cytology.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What infection is associated with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the bladder?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Schistosoma haematobium (bilharzia) — most common cause of SCC worldwide, especially in endemic areas (Egypt, sub-Saharan Africa). Chronic egg deposition → inflammation → squamous metaplasia → SCC. Also associated with chronic catheterisation and recurrent UTIs.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is adenocarcinoma of the bladder and where does it arise?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Rare (~2% of bladder cancers). Arises from urachal remnant (dome of bladder — urachal adenocarcinoma) or from bladder mucosa with intestinal metaplasia. Also secondary from colorectal, prostate, or ovarian cancer. Poor prognosis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is upper tract TCC (transitional cell carcinoma)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: TCC arising in renal pelvis or ureter. Multifocal urothelial field change — synchronous or metachronous with bladder TCC. Presents with haematuria. Managed by nephroureterectomy. Requires bladder surveillance post-operatively.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the surveillance protocol for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Low risk (single, Ta, LG, <3cm): cystoscopy at 3 months, then 12 months, then annual for 5 years. Intermediate risk: 3-monthly for 2 years, 6-monthly for 2 years, then annual. High risk (T1HG, CIS, multiple): 3-monthly for 2 years, then 6-monthly lifetime.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the mechanism of intravesical mitomycin C and when is it given?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Alkylating agent preventing DNA replication → cell death. Single instillation within 24 hours (ideally 6 hours) of TURBT reduces recurrence by 12-15% — best evidence in low-risk NMIBC. Washes out residual cells and ablates satellite lesions.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What are the complications and contraindications of BCG therapy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Complications: cystitis, haematuria, BCG sepsis (rare, treat with anti-TB drugs), pneumonitis, hepatitis. Contraindications: active TB treatment, immunosuppression (HIV, transplant), gross haematuria, recent TURBT (<2 weeks), traumatic catheterisation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the role of radical radiotherapy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Alternative to radical cystectomy in MIBC (T2-T4a). Used for unfit/patient preference. Trimodal therapy (maximal TURBT + chemotherapy + radiotherapy) offers bladder-preserving approach. 5-year survival ~40-50%, similar to cystectomy in selected patients.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What are the types of urinary diversion after radical cystectomy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Ileal conduit (Bricker): ureters anastomosed to isolated ileal segment, stoma — most common, simplest. Neobladder (orthotopic): ileal reservoir anastomosed to urethra, continent voiding. Continent cutaneous pouch (Indiana): catheterisable stoma. CIC required for pouch/neobladder.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What lymph node involvement defines N staging in bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Current TNM (7th/8th ed) is location/number-based: N1 = single node in the true pelvis; N2 = multiple nodes in the true pelvis; N3 = common iliac node(s). (Not size-based.) Node-positive disease has a poor prognosis; pelvic lymphadenectomy is performed at cystectomy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the 5-year survival for bladder cancer by stage?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Ta/T1 (NMIBC): ~80-90%. T2 (muscle-invasive, organ-confined): ~50-60%. T3 (perivesical invasion): ~30-40%. T4 (adjacent organ invasion): ~10-20%. Metastatic (M1): <5-10% at 5 years.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is MVAC chemotherapy and when is it used in bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: MVAC: Methotrexate, Vinblastine, Adriamycin (doxorubicin), Cisplatin. Used for advanced/metastatic TCC. Response rate ~40-50% but high toxicity. Now largely replaced by GC (Gemcitabine + Cisplatin) which has equivalent efficacy with better tolerability.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the role of pembrolizumab in bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Pembrolizumab: anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor — licensed for metastatic urothelial carcinoma progressing after platinum chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-045, a 2nd-line trial), and for BCG-unresponsive NMIBC. The first-line MAINTENANCE immunotherapy after a response to platinum is avelumab (JAVELIN Bladder 100), not pembrolizumab.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is PD-L1 and its significance in bladder cancer treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expressed on tumour cells inhibits T-cell cytotoxicity. PD-L1 positive tumours more likely to respond to checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, atezolizumab). PD-L1 CPS ≥10 predicts benefit in first-line unfit cisplatin patients.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the single-dose intravesical chemotherapy protocol post-TURBT?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Single instillation of mitomycin C (40 mg) or epirubicin within 24 hours (ideally 6 hours) of TURBT. Contraindicated if bladder perforation suspected (risk of systemic absorption). Reduces 5-year recurrence rate. Not given after transurethral resection for muscle-invasive disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: How do you differentiate haematuria in young vs old patients?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Young (<40): likely UTI, renal stone, IgA nephropathy, exercise-related. Older: unexplained visible haematuria is bladder/upper-tract cancer until proven otherwise. Risk rises with age, smoking and occupational exposure. NICE 2-week-wait threshold for visible haematuria is age ≥45.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is NMP22 and its role in bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Nuclear matrix protein 22 — released from nuclei of apoptotic tumour cells. Urine biomarker with sensitivity ~50-65%, specificity ~70%. FDA-approved point-of-care test. Higher sensitivity than cytology for low-grade tumours. Not widely used in UK due to limited clinical utility over cystoscopy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is blue light cystoscopy (photodynamic diagnosis) and its advantage?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Intravesical instillation of hexaminolevulinate (HAL) → fluorescent porphyrins accumulate in tumour cells → glow pink/red under blue light (380nm). Detects 20-25% more CIS and flat lesions than white light alone. Reduces recurrence rates when used at TURBT.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: How does bladder cancer cause hydronephrosis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Tumour at or near ureteric orifice (trigone/lateral wall) → ureteric obstruction → hydronephrosis. Indicates locally advanced disease (T3/T4) or large primary. Bilateral hydronephrosis = very advanced disease. Associated with worse prognosis and renal impairment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What are the squamous cell carcinoma risk factors for bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Schistosoma haematobium infection (endemic areas), chronic indwelling urinary catheter, recurrent UTI, bladder calculi, chronic irritation, smoking. SCC accounts for ~5% of bladder cancers in Western countries but up to 80% in Schistosoma-endemic regions.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What are causes of painless vs painful haematuria?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Painless: bladder cancer, renal cell carcinoma, upper tract TCC, polycystic kidney disease. Painful: renal/ureteric calculi (colicky loin pain), pyelonephritis, cystitis (stinging dysuria), clot retention (suprapubic pain). Painless visible haematuria = malignancy until proven otherwise.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is ureteric reimplantation in the context of bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Surgical reimplantation of ureter into neobladder or conduit after cystectomy. Required after excision of distal ureter (ureterectomy in upper tract TCC or cystectomy). Boari flap or psoas hitch used to bridge ureteric defects. Aim: prevent reflux and maintain drainage.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What are the indications for radical cystectomy in bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: MIBC (T2-T4a, N0-N1, M0), BCG-refractory NMIBC (high-grade T1, CIS), recurrent high-risk NMIBC. In men: removes bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles. In women: bladder, uterus, ovaries, anterior vaginal wall. Pelvic lymphadenectomy standard.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What is the Gemcitabine + Cisplatin (GC) regimen and how does it compare to MVAC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: GC: Gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² days 1, 8, 15 + Cisplatin 70 mg/m² day 1, every 28 days. Equivalent overall survival to MVAC (~13-14 months) with significantly less toxicity (less neutropenic fever, mucositis, alopecia). Now standard first-line for metastatic TCC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.front: What are the indications for neoadjuvant chemotherapy in MIBC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.back: Cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy (GC or MVAC) before radical cystectomy for T2-T4a MIBC. Level 1 evidence: improves 5-year OS by ~5-8% (absolute benefit). Eradicates micrometastases, may downstage tumour. Contraindicated if GFR <50 mL/min (cisplatin ineligibility).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: Classic triad of RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Haematuria + flank pain + palpable mass (only 10% have all 3)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What are cannonball metastases?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Well-defined circular opacities on CXR = haematogenous lung metastases from RCC

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What paraneoplastic syndrome causes polycythaemia in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Ectopic EPO secretion

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What causes left-sided varicocele in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Left testicular vein drains into left renal vein — tumour thrombus obstructs flow

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is Stauffer's syndrome?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Abnormal LFTs without liver metastases — associated with RCC (resolves after nephrectomy)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: Gold standard staging investigation for RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: CT TAP (pre + post IV contrast)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: First-line treatment for localised RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Partial or radical nephrectomy

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: Treatment for metastatic RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Sunitinib/pazopanib (TKIs) ± immunotherapy (nivolumab)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What genetic condition predisposes to bilateral RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL gene mutation)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What are the three main histological subtypes of RCC and their frequencies?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Clear cell RCC: ~75% (most common); Papillary RCC: ~15% (type 1 and type 2); Chromophobe RCC: ~5%; others include collecting duct, translocation, medullary RCC

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the pathophysiology of clear cell RCC and the role of the VHL gene?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: VHL gene (chromosome 3p25) is mutated/silenced in ~80% of sporadic clear cell RCC; VHL normally degrades HIF-1α; loss of VHL → HIF accumulation → upregulation of VEGF, PDGF, EPO → angiogenesis and tumour growth

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What are the main risk factors for RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Smoking (doubles risk), obesity (adipokines, insulin resistance), hypertension (and antihypertensives may be confounders), ADPKD (5-10x increased risk), occupational exposure (trichloroethylene), chronic renal failure, dialysis

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: How does RCC cause hypercalcaemia as a paraneoplastic syndrome?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Tumour secretion of PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein) → activates PTH receptors → bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption → hypercalcaemia; not from bone metastases per se; treat with fluids and bisphosphonates

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: How does RCC cause hypertension as a paraneoplastic syndrome?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Renin secretion by tumour → activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system → hypertension; also VEGF excess causes endothelial dysfunction; resolves after nephrectomy

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: How does RCC cause Cushing syndrome as a paraneoplastic syndrome?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Ectopic ACTH secretion by RCC → bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia → cortisol excess → Cushing syndrome (rare, <1%); features: central obesity, striae, thin skin, proximal myopathy, hypertension, diabetes

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the Robson staging system for RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Stage I: confined to kidney; Stage II: extends into perinephric fat but within Gerota fascia; Stage III: renal vein/IVC involvement or regional LN mets; Stage IV: adjacent organ invasion or distant mets; now largely replaced by TNM

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is T staging in RCC TNM classification?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: T1a: ≤4cm; T1b: 4-7cm; T2a: 7-10cm; T2b: >10cm (all confined to kidney); T3a: renal vein/perinephric fat invasion; T3b: infradiaphragmatic IVC; T3c: supradiaphragmatic IVC/heart; T4: Gerota fascia invasion

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What are the indications for partial nephrectomy versus radical nephrectomy in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Partial (nephron-sparing): imperative (solitary kidney, bilateral tumours, CKD); elective (T1a/T1b tumours with normal contralateral kidney); Radical: large T2+ tumours, hilar involvement, complex anatomy, unable to achieve clear margin with partial

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is recommended surveillance after curative nephrectomy for RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Low-risk: CT chest/abdomen at 3-6 months then annually for 3 years; High-risk: CT every 6 months for 2-3 years then annually; surveillance detects metachronous contralateral tumours and potentially resectable metastases

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is radiofrequency ablation (RFA) in RCC and when is it used?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Percutaneous or laparoscopic thermal ablation of small renal tumours (<3-4cm); used in elderly/comorbid patients unfit for surgery or those with multiple tumours; higher local recurrence than surgery; alternatives: cryoablation, HIFU

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is IVC thrombus in RCC and how is it managed?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: RCC (especially right-sided) can extend tumour thrombus into renal vein and IVC; T3b = below diaphragm IVC, T3c = above diaphragm/right atrium; managed with radical nephrectomy + IVC thrombectomy (cardiac bypass may be needed for T3c)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the Bergman sign in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Calyceal distortion or 'spider-leg' deformity on IVU/retrograde pyelogram caused by an intrarenal mass displacing collecting system; now historical sign, modern imaging (CT) has replaced IVU for RCC diagnosis

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the management of a renal incidentaloma?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: CT characterisation first: <1cm → surveillance; 1-3cm → CT/MRI at 6-12 months; suspicious features (enhancement, heterogeneity) → consider biopsy or resection; Bosniak classification for cystic lesions (I-IV); solid enhancing masses likely RCC

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is hereditary leiomyomatosis and RCC (HLRCC)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Autosomal dominant condition; FH (fumarate hydratase) gene mutation; associated with type 2 papillary RCC (aggressive), cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas; RCC often presents at young age and is treated aggressively; bevacizumab + erlotinib may be used

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is Birt-Hogg-Dubé (BHD) syndrome?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: FLCN (folliculin) gene mutation; autosomal dominant; associated with chromophobe RCC (also oncocytoma and hybrid), skin fibrofolliculomas, pulmonary cysts and spontaneous pneumothorax; renal tumours often bilateral/multifocal

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is pazopanib and how does it compare to sunitinib in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Pazopanib: oral VEGFR/PDGFR/c-KIT TKI; non-inferior to sunitinib for PFS/OS in first-line metastatic RCC; better tolerability profile (less fatigue, hand-foot syndrome) but more hepatotoxicity; COMPARZ trial: similar efficacy, preference for pazopanib

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is everolimus and its role in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin analogue); inhibits mTORC1 → reduces HIF/VEGF downstream; used in second-line after VEGFR TKI failure in metastatic RCC; side effects: stomatitis, pneumonitis, hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidaemia, immunosuppression

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is cabozantinib and its mechanism in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Multi-TKI targeting VEGFR2, MET and AXL; MET and AXL are resistance mechanisms to VEGFR inhibition; CheckMate and CABOSUN trials show superiority over sunitinib in intermediate/poor-risk patients; used first/second line mRCC

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the ipilimumab + nivolumab combination in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Dual checkpoint inhibition: ipilimumab (anti-CTLA4) + nivolumab (anti-PD1); CheckMate 214 trial: superior OS vs sunitinib in intermediate/poor-risk mRCC; now standard first-line for intermediate/poor-risk; complete responses achieved in ~10%

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the IMDC (International Metastatic RCC Database Consortium) prognostic score?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: 6 factors: KPS <80%, <1 year from diagnosis to systemic therapy, haemoglobin below LLN, calcium above ULN, neutrophils above ULN, platelets above ULN; 0 factors = favourable risk; 1-2 = intermediate; 3-6 = poor risk; guides first-line therapy choice

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the significance of renal vein involvement in RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Renal vein tumour thrombus = T3a; increases risk of haematogenous metastases (lungs, liver, bone, brain); requires radical nephrectomy with venous thrombectomy; prognosis worse than T2 but better than IVC or lymph node involvement

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the role of lymph node dissection in RCC surgery?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Routine LND does not improve survival (EORTC 30881 trial); LND performed when nodes are clinically enlarged (>1cm on CT) or for staging; lymph node metastases = N1 (any regional LN); pN1 significantly worsens prognosis

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: How is oncocytoma distinguished from RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Oncocytoma: benign tumour; CT shows homogeneous enhancement with central stellate scar (not reliable); definitive diagnosis by histology (large eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria); cannot be reliably distinguished from chromophobe RCC pre-operatively; 5% of renal tumours

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is angiomyolipoma (AML) of the kidney?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Benign hamartoma containing fat, smooth muscle and blood vessels; associated with tuberous sclerosis (80% bilateral/multiple) or sporadic; CT shows macroscopic fat (HU <-10); spontaneous haemorrhage risk >4cm → embolisation or surgery; no malignant potential in classic AML

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What does the presence of macroscopic fat on CT of a renal mass indicate?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Macroscopic fat (CT attenuation <-10 HU) within a renal mass = angiomyolipoma (AML) until proven otherwise; very rarely, fat-containing RCC (lipid-rich clear cell) can mimic this; no fat in routine RCC; if fat seen + calcification → rare fat-poor AML or RCC with engulfed perirenal fat

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is CEUS (contrast-enhanced ultrasound) in renal mass evaluation?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: CEUS uses microbubble contrast agents to assess vascularity of renal masses in real-time; no nephrotoxicity or radiation; distinguishes benign cysts (no enhancement) from solid tumours (arterial enhancement); useful in CKD, contrast allergy; Bosniak cyst classification now includes CEUS

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the Bosniak classification of renal cysts?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: I: simple benign cyst (0% malignancy); II: minimally complex (hairline septa, <3mm, ≤3 septa, ≤2 calcifications; <1% malignancy); IIF: follow-up; III: thick septa/calcification (54% malignancy) → surgical; IV: solid enhancing components (>90% malignancy) → surgical

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is the VHL gene pathway in clear cell RCC and therapeutic targeting?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: VHL loss → HIF-1α/HIF-2α accumulation → transcription of VEGF (angiogenesis), PDGF, EPO, CAIX; targeted by: VEGFR TKIs (sunitinib/pazopanib), bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), mTOR inhibitors (everolimus), HIF-2α inhibitor (belzutifan - for VHL disease)

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What are the features of papillary RCC type 1 vs type 2?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Type 1: low-grade, trisomy 7+17, MET mutations; associated with hereditary papillary RCC syndrome; better prognosis; Type 2: high-grade, diverse genomics including FH mutations (HLRCC); aggressive behaviour, poor prognosis, early metastasis

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.front: What is chromophobe RCC and why does it have a better prognosis than clear cell?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.back: Chromophobe RCC (~5%): large pale cells with prominent cell membranes; multiple chromosome losses (1,2,6,10,13,17,21); associated with BHD syndrome; generally indolent; 5-year survival ~90% for localised disease vs ~70% for clear cell; less VEGF-driven, less responsive to TKIs

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Most common cancer in males aged 20–40?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Testicular cancer

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: AFP elevated in which testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: NSGCT only — NEVER raised in pure seminoma

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: βHCG elevated in which testicular cancers?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: 60% NSGCT + 5–10% seminomas. 100% in choriocarcinoma.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Why is trans-scrotal biopsy contraindicated?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Risk of seeding cancer into inguinal lymphatics (different drainage from testicular drainage)

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Why inguinal orchidectomy (not scrotal approach)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Testicular lymphatics drain to para-aortic nodes. Scrotal approach disrupts drainage → lymph node mets in wrong territory.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Strongest risk factor for testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Cryptorchidism (undescended testes) — 10× risk even after orchidopexy

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Stage 1 testicular cancer = ?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Disease confined to testis

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What chemotherapy is used for metastatic testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: BEP — Bleomycin + Etoposide + Cisplatin

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Why must fertility be assessed before testicular cancer treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Chemotherapy/radiotherapy cause infertility — cryopreservation offered to all patients

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What are the two main histological types of testicular germ cell tumours?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Seminoma (most common ~50%): radiosensitive, slow-growing, peaks 25–35 years. Non-seminomatous germ cell tumour (NSGCT ~50%): mixed types (embryonal, teratoma, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma), more aggressive, peaks 15–30 years.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the classic presentation of testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Painless testicular swelling/lump — the key exam feature (painless). May have dull ache. Hydrocele in 10%. Occasionally presents with metastatic features (back pain from retroperitoneal LN, gynaecomastia from hCG, haemoptysis from lung mets).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the first-line investigation for a testicular lump?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Testicular USS — first-line, highly sensitive/specific. Distinguishes intratesticular (likely malignant) from extratesticular (usually benign). Never biopsy through the scrotum — risk of lymphatic seeding.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What are the tumour markers for testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: AFP (alpha-fetoprotein), beta-hCG, LDH. AFP raised in NSGCT (especially yolk sac); NEVER raised in pure seminoma — if AFP raised, treat as NSGCT regardless of histology. Beta-hCG raised in NSGCT and ~20% seminomas. LDH = tumour bulk marker.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Why is AFP never elevated in pure seminoma?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Seminoma cells do not produce AFP. If AFP is raised after orchidectomy in a supposedly 'pure seminoma', there must be an occult NSGCT component — treat as NSGCT (more aggressive protocol).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the definitive diagnostic and initial therapeutic procedure for testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Radical inguinal orchidectomy — inguinal approach (NOT scrotal; avoids disrupting lymphatic drainage and seeding to inguinal nodes). Provides diagnosis, staging, and removes primary tumour.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: Why must testicular biopsy and orchidectomy be performed via an inguinal (not scrotal) incision?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Testicular lymphatics drain to para-aortic lymph nodes (not inguinal). Scrotal incision alters lymphatic drainage to inguinal nodes, complicating staging and spreading disease to a new nodal territory, making surgery and radiotherapy more complex.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What staging investigations are performed for testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (para-aortic nodes, lung mets). Tumour markers (AFP, hCG, LDH — pre- and post-orchidectomy). MRI brain if CNS symptoms. PET-CT for seminoma residual mass post-chemotherapy. Stage by TNM + IGCCCG risk group.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the management of Stage I seminoma?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Radical inguinal orchidectomy + surveillance (most UK centres) OR single-dose carboplatin chemotherapy OR para-aortic radiotherapy. Surveillance preferred (excellent cure rates). Cure rate >99%.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the management of Stage I NSGCT?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Radical inguinal orchidectomy + surveillance (if good compliance, low-risk features) OR adjuvant BEP × 1–2 cycles. Surveillance with regular CT and tumour markers (AFP, hCG falls after orchidectomy — if plateaus, residual disease).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is BEP chemotherapy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Bleomycin + Etoposide + Cisplatin — the backbone of testicular cancer chemotherapy. Used for metastatic and high-risk stage I testicular cancer. Bleomycin toxicity: pulmonary fibrosis (major concern — monitor PFTs).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What are the risk factors for testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis — 5× increased risk, remains elevated even after orchidopexy, but orchidopexy allows self-examination). Family history (1st degree — 8–10× risk). Klinefelter's syndrome. Contralateral testicular cancer.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the importance of cryptorchidism in relation to testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Undescended testis: 5× increased risk of testicular cancer, even if orchidopexy performed. Orchidopexy (recommended before age 2) brings testis into scrotum for self-examination. Both the undescended AND contralateral testis have elevated risk.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What lymph node group is involved in testicular cancer metastasis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Para-aortic (retroperitoneal) lymph nodes — because testicular lymphatics follow the testicular vessels to their embryological origin. Inguinal nodes only involved if scrotal skin infiltrated or prior scrotal surgery disrupted drainage.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the prognosis of testicular cancer overall?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Excellent — ~95–98% overall cure rate. Stage I: >99% cure. Even metastatic (Stage III) good-prognosis category has ~90% cure with BEP. Most curable solid tumour in young men. Lance Armstrong famously survived stage III with lung, brain, abdominal mets.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is a teratoma (in the context of testicular tumours in adults)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: In UK oncology convention, 'teratoma' = NSGCT in adults (covering all non-seminomatous elements). Contains differentiated tissue from two or more germ layers. Malignant (unlike paediatric teratomas which can be benign). Treated as NSGCT.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is gynaecomastia as a presentation of testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Beta-hCG from testicular tumour acts on breast tissue → gynaecomastia. Seen especially with choriocarcinoma (high hCG producer) and mixed NSGCT. Should prompt testicular examination. Also causes back pain (retroperitoneal LN), haemoptysis (lung mets).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Surgical removal of para-aortic retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Used in Stage II NSGCT (after chemotherapy for residual masses). Risk of ejaculatory dysfunction (retrograde ejaculation) from sympathetic nerve injury — nerve-sparing technique preferred.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: When is PET-CT used in testicular cancer staging?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: For residual retroperitoneal mass after chemotherapy in seminoma — PET-CT distinguishes viable tumour (FDG-avid, requires surgery/further treatment) from necrosis/fibrosis (PET-negative, safe to observe). NOT reliable for NSGCT residual masses.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What fertility preservation advice should be given before testicular cancer treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Sperm banking before orchidectomy and/or chemotherapy — essential. Chemotherapy (BEP) can cause azoospermia/infertility. Radiotherapy also affects fertility. Unilateral orchidectomy alone usually preserves fertility, but discuss and offer sperm cryopreservation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What are the long-term side effects of BEP chemotherapy for testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Bleomycin: pulmonary fibrosis (monitor PFTs); avoid high FiO2 anaesthesia post-BEP. Cisplatin: nephrotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, ototoxicity, secondary malignancies (leukaemia). Etoposide: secondary AML. Cardiovascular risk increased long-term.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the IGCCCG risk classification for testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group: Good, Intermediate, Poor prognosis based on tumour markers (AFP, hCG, LDH levels), histology, and primary site. Good prognosis (both seminoma and NSGCT) = ~90% 5-year survival. Poor prognosis NSGCT = ~50%.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is a hydrocele in the context of testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Secondary hydrocele (fluid around testis) can develop in 10% of testicular cancers — may mask the underlying tumour on examination. All new hydroceles in young men should have USS to exclude underlying malignancy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is a contralateral biopsy and when is it recommended?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Biopsy of opposite testis at time of orchidectomy: considered in high-risk patients (small testis <12 mL, cryptorchidism, infertility) — detects carcinoma in situ (GCNIS)/intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN) at 5%. Treatment: low-dose testicular irradiation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What causes Leydig cell tumours and how do they differ from germ cell tumours?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Leydig cell tumours: sex-cord stromal tumours, NOT germ cell tumours. Secrete androgens/oestrogens. Present with gynaecomastia, precocious puberty (children). Tumour markers (AFP, hCG) negative. Mostly benign; radical orchidectomy curative. Rare (<3% testicular tumours).

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the 5-year survival for stage I vs stage III testicular cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Stage I: >99%. Stage II (lymph node involvement): ~95%. Stage III (distant metastases, good prognosis): ~90%. Stage III poor prognosis: ~50–60%. Overall: ~97% — testicular cancer has the highest cure rate of all solid tumours.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is the treatment for choriocarcinoma (a subtype of NSGCT)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Most aggressive NSGCT — haematogenous spread early, very high hCG. Treatment: immediate BEP chemotherapy. Often presents with pulmonary/brain metastases at diagnosis. Despite aggressive biology, responds well to platinum-based chemotherapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What must be done if AFP or hCG fails to normalise after orchidectomy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Failure of tumour markers to normalise suggests residual disease — requires staging CT and consideration of chemotherapy (BEP). Markers should fall with their known half-lives: AFP ~5 days, hCG ~1–2 days. Plateau or rise = persistent/metastatic disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What is germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Previously CIS or ITGCN — precursor lesion to invasive germ cell tumours. Found in 5% of men with risk factors (contralateral tumour, cryptorchidism). Progresses to invasive tumour in ~50% at 5 years. Treated with low-dose radiotherapy to affected testis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: What investigation monitors for tumour recurrence after testicular cancer treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Regular tumour markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) + CT chest/abdomen/pelvis at scheduled intervals (surveillance protocols vary by stage/histology). Surveillance for 5–10 years. Self-examination of remaining testis. CXR at some visits.

conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the key facts about testicular cancer for finals?
conditions__UROLOGY__Testicular Cancer.back: Painless testicular lump in young man. USS first-line. Inguinal orchidectomy (NOT scrotal biopsy). Markers: AFP (NSGCT only), hCG (both), LDH (bulk). Spread to para-aortic nodes. BEP chemotherapy. Excellent prognosis (~97% overall). Cryptorchidism is main risk factor.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Trimethoprim 200mg BD × 3 days
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Simple LUTI in young woman — trimethoprim 3 days is first-line.
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 25-year-old woman has dysuria, frequency, and urine dipstick positive for nitrites and leucocytes. Best treatment?

options: Treat only if she becomes symptomatic
Observation — asymptomatic bacteriuria does not require treatment
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: 7-day course of cefalexin (after sensitivities)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: All pregnant women with bacteriuria must be treated — risk of pyelonephritis + preterm labour.
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 10 weeks has asymptomatic bacteriuria confirmed on MSU. Management?

options: Folate antagonist → risk of neural tube defects
It is teratogenic at all stages
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Folate antagonist → risk of neural tube defects
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase → folate deficiency → NTDs in 1st trimester.
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: Why should trimethoprim be avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy?

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Do NOT treat as UTI
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Leucocytes alone = inflammation — does not confirm infection. Check for other causes.
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: Urine dipstick shows leucocytes ONLY (no nitrites, no haematuria). What is the appropriate action?

A 24-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of dysuria, increased urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She is apyrexial. Urine dipstick is positive for leucocytes and nitrites. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Send MSU and await culture before treating
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Trimethoprim 200 mg BD for 3 days
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant woman: NICE recommends a 3-day course of nitrofurantoin (or trimethoprim where local resistance is low) as first-line. No systemic features → oral treatment; typical symptoms plus a positive dipstick are sufficient, without awaiting culture.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 28-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation has an MSU at booking showing >105 CFU/mL of E. coli with no urinary symptoms. What is the correct management?
options: Treat with appropriate antibiotics (e.g. nitrofurantoin if sensitive, avoid in 3rd trimester) — asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated
Reassure — asymptomatic bacteriuria requires no treatment
Repeat MSU in 4 weeks — too early to treat
IV antibiotics — any infection in pregnancy requires IV route
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Treat with appropriate antibiotics (e.g. nitrofurantoin if sensitive, avoid in 3rd trimester) — asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated — unlike non-pregnant patients. Risk of ascending pyelonephritis (~30% without treatment), preterm labour, and low birth weight. Nitrofurantoin safe in 1st/2nd trimester; avoid near term (neonatal haemolysis). Trimethoprim avoided in 1st trimester (folate antagonist). Screen all pregnant women at booking.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 68-year-old diabetic woman presents with high fever, rigors, right loin pain, and tender right renal angle. Urine dipstick: positive leucocytes, nitrites. BP 90/55, HR 120, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: IV antibiotics (e.g. gentamicin or piperacillin-tazobactam) + IV fluids + blood cultures + urgent renal imaging
Admit and start IV fluids only
NSAIDs for loin pain and send MSU to GP
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: IV antibiotics (e.g. gentamicin or piperacillin-tazobactam) + IV fluids + blood cultures + urgent renal imaging
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Pyelonephritis with septic shock criteria (hypotension, tachycardia, raised lactate) in a diabetic patient: IV antibiotics + Sepsis Six bundle + imaging (CT KUB) to exclude obstruction/complication (emphysematous pyelonephritis is a risk in diabetics). Blood cultures before antibiotics. ICU if not responding.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 70-year-old man has a urinary catheter in situ for urinary retention. MSU grows >105 CFU/mL of Klebsiella pneumoniae. He is afebrile, comfortable, and has no urinary symptoms. What is the appropriate action?
options: No antibiotic treatment — this is asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient; change catheter if due for replacement
Remove catheter and observe — treat only if symptoms develop
Refer to microbiology for prolonged antibiotic course
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: No antibiotic treatment — this is asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient; change catheter if due for replacement
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients should NOT be treated with antibiotics (except before urological procedures or in pregnancy/transplant recipients). Treatment increases antibiotic resistance and adverse effects without clinical benefit. Change the catheter if due. Treat only if systemic symptoms of infection develop.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 35-year-old woman has had 4 UTIs in the past year, all caused by E. coli sensitive to trimethoprim. She has had no structural urological abnormalities on USS. What is the most appropriate long-term management strategy?
options: Low-dose prophylactic trimethoprim 100 mg nightly OR post-coital single dose (if coitus-related)
No treatment — recurrent UTI is not a medical problem
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Low-dose prophylactic trimethoprim 100 mg nightly OR post-coital single dose (if coitus-related)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Recurrent UTI (≥3/year) without structural cause in women: antibiotic prophylaxis (low-dose trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin nightly, or post-coital) for 6 months is appropriate after non-antibiotic measures (fluids, voiding advice, cranberry, D-mannose). Alternative: patient-initiated self-start therapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: Which antibiotic should be AVOIDED in uncomplicated lower UTI in a woman with eGFR of 35 mL/min?
options: Nitrofurantoin — ineffective when eGFR <45 mL/min (inadequate urinary concentration) and risk of systemic accumulation
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Nitrofurantoin — ineffective when eGFR <45 mL/min (inadequate urinary concentration) and risk of systemic accumulation
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Nitrofurantoin acts by achieving high urinary concentrations. Below eGFR 45 mL/min: insufficient urinary concentration → treatment failure. Also risk of systemic accumulation → peripheral neuropathy, pulmonary toxicity. Use trimethoprim or cefalexin for lower UTI in CKD (avoiding trimethoprim if K+ high).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 6-month-old boy presents with a temperature of 39°C, vomiting, and poor feeding. MSU (catheter sample) grows E. coli >105 CFU/mL. What investigation should be arranged urgently?
options: Renal ultrasound (within 6 weeks; during the acute infection if atypical/seriously unwell) — NICE: infants <6 months with a UTI need a USS to exclude a structural abnormality
Await 4 weeks — first UTI in young child is usually benign
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Renal ultrasound (within 6 weeks; during the acute infection if atypical/seriously unwell) — NICE: infants <6 months with a UTI need a USS to exclude a structural abnormality
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: NICE CG54: infants <6 months with a first UTI should have a renal USS — during the acute infection if the UTI is atypical or the child is seriously unwell, otherwise within 6 weeks. A DMSA scan (4–6 months later) assesses renal scarring in recurrent/atypical UTI; MCUG is considered if VUR or obstruction is suspected.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: Which organism is the second most common cause of UTI in sexually active young women and has a characteristic presentation?
options: Staphylococcus saprophyticus — causes acute cystitis in sexually active young women, MSU shows Gram-positive cocci
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Staphylococcus saprophyticus — causes acute cystitis in sexually active young women, MSU shows Gram-positive cocci
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: S. saprophyticus is the 2nd most common UTI pathogen in sexually active young women (E. coli is first). Coagulase-negative Staph, novobiocin-resistant. Typical history: young woman with dysuria and frequency after sexual activity. Treat with trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin (usually sensitive).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 65-year-old diabetic woman presents with severe left loin pain, fever 39.5°C, and rigors. CT KUB shows gas within the left renal parenchyma. What is the diagnosis and its management?
options: Emphysematous pyelonephritis — IV antibiotics + urgent percutaneous nephrostomy ± nephrectomy
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Emphysematous pyelonephritis — IV antibiotics + urgent percutaneous nephrostomy ± nephrectomy
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Emphysematous pyelonephritis: gas-forming infection of renal parenchyma, almost exclusively in diabetics. Gas on CT = diagnostic. Life-threatening (20–40% mortality). IV antibiotics + urgent drainage (nephrostomy) is key — some require nephrectomy. ICU involvement. Mortality highest with bilateral disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman has had 4 UTIs in the last year since her menopause. She has no structural urological abnormality. What is the most appropriate preventive treatment?
options: Topical vaginal oestrogen (pessary or cream) — reduces recurrence by 60–70%
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Topical vaginal oestrogen (pessary or cream) — reduces recurrence by 60–70%
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Post-menopausal UTI: oestrogen deficiency causes vaginal atrophy, reduced lactobacilli, alkaline pH → uropathogens colonise vagina. Topical vaginal oestrogen restores vaginal flora → reduces UTI recurrence by ~60-70%. Systemic HRT does not have proven UTI prevention benefit. First-line before prophylactic antibiotics in postmenopausal women.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: What is the correct interpretation of a urine dipstick showing positive leucocyte esterase and negative nitrites?
options: Could be a non-E. coli UTI (e.g. Staphylococcus — doesn't produce nitrites); send MSU for culture
Rules out UTI — both must be positive
Confirms non-infectious cause of dysuria (e.g. interstitial cystitis)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Could be a non-E. coli UTI (e.g. Staphylococcus — doesn't produce nitrites); send MSU for culture
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Positive leucocyte esterase (pyuria) + negative nitrites: not all uropathogens are nitrite-producers (Gram-positive organisms, Pseudomonas, fungi). Also: dilute urine, rapid transit reduces nitrite conversion. Send MSU for culture. Treat if symptoms are consistent with UTI and clinical picture supports infection.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 45-year-old man presents with his first episode of UTI symptoms — dysuria, frequency, and a tender prostate on DRE. MSU grows E. coli. What is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
options: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 14 days (fluoroquinolone for prostate penetration)
Trimethoprim 200 mg BD for 7 days (standard female regimen)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 14 days (fluoroquinolone for prostate penetration)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: UTI in a man = complicated UTI; tender prostate on DRE = acute prostatitis. Ciprofloxacin (14–28 days) or trimethoprim (14 days) — need good prostate penetration. Fluoroquinolones are preferred for acute bacterial prostatitis. Standard 7-day female regimen is inadequate. Investigate with USS and PSA after resolution.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: What is the mechanism by which D-mannose may prevent recurrent E. coli UTIs?
options: D-mannose binds E. coli type 1 fimbriae (pili), blocking adhesion to urothelium
D-mannose is metabolised by E. coli, slowing growth
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: D-mannose binds E. coli type 1 fimbriae (pili), blocking adhesion to urothelium
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: E. coli adheres to urothelial cells via type 1 fimbriae (mannose-sensitive). D-mannose competitively inhibits this adhesion by binding fimbrial tip adhesins — bacteria cannot attach and are washed out. Safe, well-tolerated, modest evidence for UTI prevention. Alternative to antibiotics for recurrent UTI.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 78-year-old woman with an indwelling urethral catheter develops confusion, fever 38.5°C, and hypotension. MSU from catheter grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. What is the correct management?
options: Blood cultures, IV antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam), change catheter, Sepsis Six bundle
Send MSU and await results before treating
Remove catheter only — no antibiotics needed
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Blood cultures, IV antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam), change catheter, Sepsis Six bundle
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: CAUTI with systemic features (sepsis criteria) = severe infection requiring urgent treatment. Sepsis Six within 1 hour. IV antibiotics covering Pseudomonas (Tazocin or meropenem depending on local resistance). Change catheter (removes biofilm reservoir). Blood cultures before antibiotics. ITU review if haemodynamically unstable.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with dysuria. She has a urethral discharge and her partner was recently treated for gonorrhoea. Urine dipstick is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: STI screen (NAAT swabs for chlamydia/gonorrhoea) — urethritis NOT cystitis
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: STI screen (NAAT swabs for chlamydia/gonorrhoea) — urethritis NOT cystitis
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Dysuria + urethral discharge + negative dipstick + STI contact = sexually transmitted urethritis. Urethral discharge distinguishes this from cystitis. Treat with STI antibiotics (doxycycline for chlamydia, ceftriaxone for gonorrhoea). Refer to GUM clinic. MSU negative or low count. Do NOT give trimethoprim without STI screen.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: Which of the following correctly describes vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and its long-term consequence?
options: Retrograde urine flow to kidney during voiding → recurrent pyelonephritis → reflux nephropathy (renal scarring) → hypertension and CKD
Forward flow from kidney to bladder — protective against UTI
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Retrograde urine flow to kidney during voiding → recurrent pyelonephritis → reflux nephropathy (renal scarring) → hypertension and CKD
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: VUR: abnormal retrograde urine flow from bladder to ureter/kidney during voiding. Grades I–V. Recurrent UTIs cause repeated episodes of pyelonephritis → renal cortical scarring (reflux nephropathy) → reduced GFR, hypertension, CKD in severe cases. Screen children with recurrent UTIs (USS, DMSA, MCUG for high grade VUR).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 62-year-old diabetic man presents with recurrent urinary symptoms and an MSU that grows Candida albicans. He is asymptomatic with a stable glycaemic control. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Remove urinary catheter (if present) and optimise glycaemic control — treat antifungals only if symptomatic or immunocompromised
No action needed — Candida is a contaminant
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Remove urinary catheter (if present) and optimise glycaemic control — treat antifungals only if symptomatic or immunocompromised
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic candiduria in non-immunocompromised patients: remove catheter (often clears spontaneously), optimise glucose control, change antibiotics if on broad-spectrum. Antifungal treatment only if: symptomatic, immunocompromised (renal transplant, neutropaenic), before urological procedures, or neonates. Fluconazole is first-line if treatment indicated.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 50-year-old woman has had a renal transplant and is on immunosuppression. She develops asymptomatic bacteriuria 2 months post-transplant. What is the correct management?
options: Treat with targeted antibiotics — asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in transplant recipients in the first 3–6 months post-transplant
Observe — asymptomatic bacteriuria never requires treatment
IV antibiotics for 14 days regardless of organism
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Treat with targeted antibiotics — asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in transplant recipients in the first 3–6 months post-transplant
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Renal transplant recipients: asymptomatic bacteriuria treated in first 3–6 months post-transplant (unlike general population) — risk of pyelonephritis of transplanted kidney, graft dysfunction, and rejection. After 6 months, management similar to general population if no special risk factors. Choose antibiotics carefully to avoid drug interactions with immunosuppressants.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 25-year-old woman gets UTI symptoms after every episode of sexual intercourse. MSU consistently grows E. coli. What is the most appropriate preventive strategy?
options: Post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis (single dose trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin after intercourse)
Daily antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of coitus
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis (single dose trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin after intercourse)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Coitus-related recurrent UTI: post-coital single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis is the most targeted and effective strategy. Trimethoprim 100 mg or nitrofurantoin 50 mg post-coitus prevents colonisation from mechanical inoculation. Non-antibiotic measures also important: post-coital voiding, adequate hydration, D-mannose.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: What is the most appropriate investigation when a patient fails to respond to antibiotics for a UTI?
options: MSU culture and sensitivity + USS KUB to exclude obstruction or complicated UTI
CT head to exclude CNS cause of symptoms
No investigation — reassure and prescribe different antibiotic empirically
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: MSU culture and sensitivity + USS KUB to exclude obstruction or complicated UTI
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Treatment failure in UTI: MSU C&S to identify resistant organism and guide antibiotic change. USS KUB to exclude obstruction (stone, tumour causing stasis), abscess, or structural abnormality. Consider: wrong diagnosis (STI, interstitial cystitis), resistant organism, inadequate treatment duration, or complicated UTI.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: EXAM PEARL: What are the three clinical situations in which asymptomatic bacteriuria MUST be treated?
options: Pregnancy, before urological procedures (risk of sepsis), and renal transplant recipients (first 3–6 months)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Pregnancy, before urological procedures (risk of sepsis), and renal transplant recipients (first 3–6 months)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is NOT treated in most patients — risks antibiotic resistance and adverse effects. MUST treat in: (1) Pregnancy — risk of pyelonephritis/preterm labour; (2) Before urological procedures (TURP, cystoscopy) — prevent procedure-induced bacteraemia; (3) Renal transplant recipients (first 3–6 months) — risk of graft pyelonephritis. This is a classic OSCE/exam question.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: Which of the following is the most common healthcare-associated infection?
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: CAUTI is the most common healthcare-associated infection (HAI) — accounting for ~40% of hospital-acquired infections. Pathogenesis: biofilm formation on catheter, extraluminal (most) or intraluminal contamination. Prevention: avoid unnecessary catheterisation, aseptic insertion, closed drainage, early removal. Use TWOC (trial without catheter) as soon as clinically feasible.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 20-year-old woman with a 3-day history of dysuria, frequency, and haematuria has a positive urine dipstick for nitrites and leucocytes. She is apyrexial and well. She is 8 weeks pregnant. What antibiotic is safest?
options: Nitrofurantoin 50 mg QDS for 7 days (safe in 1st/2nd trimester)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Nitrofurantoin 50 mg QDS for 7 days (safe in 1st/2nd trimester)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Antibiotic safety in pregnancy: Nitrofurantoin safe in 1st/2nd trimester (avoid at term — neonatal haemolysis). Trimethoprim avoided in 1st trimester (folate antagonist → neural tube defects). Cefalexin is another safe option throughout pregnancy. Ciprofloxacin, tetracyclines, and aminoglycosides are avoided unless no alternatives.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: What is the significance of proteinuria found on urine dipstick during investigation for recurrent UTIs?
options: Should be re-checked 2–4 weeks after UTI resolution — persistent proteinuria suggests underlying renal disease (reflux nephropathy, glomerulonephritis)
Proteinuria during active UTI is always benign — no follow-up needed
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Should be re-checked 2–4 weeks after UTI resolution — persistent proteinuria suggests underlying renal disease (reflux nephropathy, glomerulonephritis)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Proteinuria during active UTI (pyuria, bacteriuria) can be a transient finding from inflammation. Re-check dipstick 4–6 weeks post-treatment. Persistent proteinuria = glomerulonephritis, reflux nephropathy, diabetic nephropathy, or other renal disease — refer for further investigation (ACR, renal function, USS).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 75-year-old woman in a care home has a urinary catheter. She is confused but this is her baseline. MSU from catheter grows E. coli 106 CFU/mL. Temperature 36.8°C, BP and HR normal. What is the correct management?
options: No antibiotics — this is asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient; address non-infectious causes of confusion
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: No antibiotics — this is asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient; address non-infectious causes of confusion
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient does NOT require antibiotics — even with baseline confusion. This is a classic over-treatment scenario. MSU from catheters frequently grows organisms (>90% have bacteriuria at 30 days). Treat only if systemic signs of infection. Investigate confusion for other causes (medication, constipation, pain, metabolic).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: EXAM PEARL: A 28-year-old woman has her 4th UTI this year. USS KUB is normal. She is postcoitally affected. What is the first-line non-antibiotic strategy, and when should prophylaxis be offered?
options: Non-antibiotic: increase fluid intake, post-coital voiding, D-mannose, topical oestrogen if postmenopausal; prophylaxis offered if ≥3 UTIs/year after non-antibiotic measures fail
Non-antibiotic measures have no evidence — start prophylaxis immediately
Lifelong high-dose antibiotics from first recurrence
Only post-coital antibiotics, no other measures have evidence
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Non-antibiotic: increase fluid intake, post-coital voiding, D-mannose, topical oestrogen if postmenopausal; prophylaxis offered if ≥3 UTIs/year after non-antibiotic measures fail
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: NICE/EAU guidelines: Non-antibiotic measures first (hydration, voiding habits, D-mannose, cranberry with limited evidence, topical oestrogen postmenopausally). Offer antibiotic prophylaxis (low-dose trimethoprim/nitrofurantoin nightly, or post-coital) if ≥3 UTIs in 12 months or ≥2 in 6 months after non-antibiotic measures. Patient self-start therapy is an alternative to continuous prophylaxis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman has a midstream urine showing >10^5 CFU/mL E. coli with no symptoms. What is the appropriate management?
options: Treat with antibiotics — asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy requires treatment to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth
No treatment needed as she is asymptomatic
Monitor and treat only if she develops symptoms
Give prophylactic low-dose nitrofurantoin throughout pregnancy
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is an exception to the rule (in non-pregnant women, it is generally not treated). In pregnancy, it carries a 25-40% risk of progressing to pyelonephritis (due to ureteric dilatation/immunosuppression) and is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight. Treat based on sensitivity (amoxicillin/nitrofurantoin/cefalexin).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 70-year-old man with a long-term urinary catheter has a urine culture showing E. coli >10^5 CFU/mL. He is afebrile with no symptoms. What is the appropriate management?
options: No antibiotics — catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated (increases resistance)
Treat with a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin
Perform CT KUB to exclude renal involvement
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients should NOT be treated with antibiotics (except before urological procedures or in pregnancy). Treatment does not reduce symptoms or complications but increases antibiotic resistance and Clostridium difficile risk. Remove/change catheter where possible.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: Which antibiotic is contraindicated for UTI treatment in the first trimester of pregnancy and at term?
options: Trimethoprim (folate antagonist — teratogenic in first trimester; avoid at term)
Nitrofurantoin (safe in pregnancy except at term — haemolytic anaemia risk in neonate)
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist — teratogenic in the first trimester (risk of neural tube defects) and should be avoided at term (folate deficiency risk). Nitrofurantoin is safe in pregnancy except at term (risk of neonatal haemolytic anaemia from G6PD deficiency). Cefalexin and amoxicillin (if sensitive) are generally safe.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 35-year-old woman has her third UTI in the past year. Urine cultures consistently grow E. coli. She is otherwise well with no structural abnormality on USS. What is the appropriate management strategy?
options: Long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., trimethoprim 100 mg nocte) or post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis
Treat each episode as it occurs only
No treatment as frequent UTIs are normal in women
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Recurrent UTIs in women (>=3/year or >=2 in 6 months) can be managed with: long-term prophylactic low-dose antibiotics (trimethoprim 100 mg nocte or nitrofurantoin 50 mg nocte), post-coital antibiotics (if coitus-related), self-start therapy, or behavioural measures (cranberry, hydration, voiding after sex).

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: What is the most appropriate antibiotic for uncomplicated UTI in women according to NICE guidelines?
options: Nitrofurantoin (if eGFR >45 mL/min) or trimethoprim as first-line for 3 days
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: NICE recommends nitrofurantoin (3-5 days, if eGFR >45) or trimethoprim (3 days, if local resistance <20%) as first-line for uncomplicated UTIs in women. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) are reserved for complicated/systemic infections to preserve their activity. Amoxicillin has high E. coli resistance rates.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 65-year-old man develops fever, rigors and severe right-sided loin pain 3 days after a ureteric stent insertion for a stone. His BP is 90/60 mmHg. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Urosepsis — septic shock from obstructed infected kidney: emergency percutaneous nephrostomy or stent revision plus IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluid resuscitation
Renal colic from stent migration — analgesia
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Obstructed infected kidney + septic shock = urological emergency. The obstructed system acts as a pus under pressure reservoir. Emergency decompression (percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent) + IV antibiotics (tazobactam, gentamicin) + sepsis 6 bundle. Delay is life-threatening.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: What is emphysematous pyelonephritis?
options: Necrotising gas-forming infection of the renal parenchyma — occurs in diabetics, associated with E. coli; high mortality
Pyelonephritis with emphysema as a comorbidity
Renal abscess with gas from fistula to bowel
UTI with pneumaturia in catheterised patients
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: Necrotising gas-forming infection of the renal parenchyma — occurs in diabetics, associated with E. coli; high mortality
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a necrotising gas-forming renal infection caused by E. coli (or Klebsiella), occurring almost exclusively in diabetics; CT shows gas in the renal parenchyma and mortality is high. First-line treatment is IV antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage and supportive care; nephrectomy is reserved for failure of drainage or extensive disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 24-year-old man presents with dysuria, urethral discharge and a tender swollen epididymis. What organisms should be covered in treatment?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae — doxycycline + ceftriaxone pending culture
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: In sexually active young men, epididymo-orchitis is usually sexually transmitted (Chlamydia, gonorrhoea). Treatment: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM (gonorrhoea) + doxycycline 100 mg BD x 10-14 days (Chlamydia) pending cultures. In older men, E. coli is more common (treat with quinolone). Screen and treat sexual contacts.

conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.question: A 78-year-old woman with dementia has confusion and behavioural change. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leukocytes. Urine culture grows E. coli >10^5 CFU/mL. She has no urinary symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Investigate thoroughly for other causes of confusion before attributing to UTI — asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in elderly women
Immediately start antibiotics for UTI as bacteria in urine confirms UTI
Catheterise to prevent contamination of future specimens
Empirically treat with trimethoprim as 'confusion is a UTI symptom in the elderly'
Transfer to hospital for IV antibiotics
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.answer: A
conditions__UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infec.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is very common in elderly women (up to 50%) and should generally not be treated. Confusion in the elderly has multiple causes (delirium from medications, metabolic causes, infection elsewhere). Attributing all confusion to UTI is a common clinical error. Thorough assessment for other causes of delirium is required.
