conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Retrograde ejaculation affects 65-90% of men post-TURP due to disruption of bladder neck/external sphincter coordination. Semen enters the bladder instead of being expelled antegrade. Must be discussed pre-operatively.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: During TURP, a patient develops confusion, hypertension, and bradycardia. Serum sodium is 122 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: TUR syndrome: absorption of hypotonic glycine irrigant during TURP → dilutional hyponatraemia (<125 mmol/L). Presents with CNS symptoms (confusion, visual disturbance), cardiovascular instability. Risk >1 hour resection time. Treat with hypertonic saline if severe.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A man with a prostate volume of 120 mL is planned for surgical treatment of BPH. Which procedure is most appropriate?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: HoLEP is size-independent and preferred for large prostates (>80-100 mL). Standard TURP is limited by resection time (increased TUR syndrome risk >1 hour) and is less suitable for very large glands. HoLEP has equivalent outcomes to open prostatectomy with less morbidity.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: Which enzyme does finasteride inhibit in BPH treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase type 2 (predominant in prostate), preventing conversion of testosterone to DHT. Dutasteride inhibits both type 1 and 2. DHT reduction leads to prostate volume reduction (~20-30%) over 6 months.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 70-year-old with BPH has a Qmax of 8 mL/s on uroflowmetry. What does this suggest?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Qmax <10 mL/s suggests significant outflow obstruction (normal >15 mL/s). However, uroflowmetry requires >150 mL voided volume and cannot distinguish obstruction from poor detrusor contractility — urodynamics needed for definitive assessment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 65-year-old with BPH presents with frank haematuria. He has no dysuria or fever. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: A. Flexible cystoscopy and CT urogram
B. Reassurance as haematuria is common in BPH
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Frank haematuria must never be attributed to BPH without excluding bladder cancer and upper tract TCC. NICE guidelines mandate flexible cystoscopy + CT urogram via 2-week wait haematuria clinic for all patients with visible haematuria.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What is the correct approach to post-obstructive diuresis following catheterisation for high-pressure chronic retention?
options: A. Replace 50% of hourly urine output with IV fluids
B. Restrict all IV fluids to prevent worsening diuresis
C. Clamp catheter when output exceeds 200 mL/hour
D. Administer DDAVP to reduce urine output
E. Nephrology referral before any fluid replacement
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Post-obstructive diuresis can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. Replace 50% of urine output (not 1:1, as some diuresis is physiologically appropriate — clearing retained solutes). Monitor electrolytes 4-6 hourly.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A patient has a failed TWOC 48 hours after acute retention. He was started on tamsulosin at catheter insertion. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Re-catheterise and arrange urology review for TURP
C. Switch to a 5-ARI and attempt TWOC in 6 months
E. Urgent urodynamics before any further management
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Failed TWOC after adequate alpha blocker treatment (at least 48 hours pre-TWOC) is an indication for surgical intervention (usually TURP). Re-catheterisation provides symptom relief while awaiting definitive surgery. A second TWOC has low success rate.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: Which alpha blocker is most associated with intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract surgery?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Tamsulosin (highly selective alpha-1A) causes IFIS during cataract surgery — iris dilator muscle relaxation leads to progressive pupil constriction, iris prolapse, and billowing. Must inform ophthalmologist before surgery; may require modified surgical technique.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 66-year-old presents with gynaecomastia and reduced libido 18 months after starting finasteride. What is the cause?
options: A. Side effects of 5-alpha reductase inhibition
D. Drug interaction with concurrent alpha blocker
E. Idiopathic hormonal change unrelated to medication
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: 5-ARIs (finasteride, dutasteride) reduce DHT → relative oestrogen excess → gynaecomastia (2%) and breast tenderness. Reduced libido and erectile dysfunction also occur. Discontinuation usually reverses symptoms but post-finasteride syndrome (persistent effects) is described.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What is the mechanism by which tadalafil improves LUTS in BPH?
options: A. PDE5 inhibition increasing cGMP in prostate/bladder neck smooth muscle
B. Alpha-1A receptor blockade in prostate stroma
D. Muscarinic receptor blockade reducing detrusor overactivity
E. Beta-3 adrenoceptor agonism increasing bladder capacity
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Tadalafil inhibits PDE5, preventing cGMP breakdown → sustained smooth muscle relaxation in the prostate, urethra, and bladder neck via nitric oxide/cGMP pathway. Licensed for both erectile dysfunction and LUTS at 5 mg daily.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 75-year-old man with BPH has IPSS 9 and is bothered by nocturia twice nightly. He is otherwise well with no complications. What is first-line management?
options: A. Watchful waiting with lifestyle advice
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: IPSS 8-19 is moderate, but with minimal bother and no complications (no retention, infection, stones, renal impairment), watchful waiting with lifestyle measures (fluid restriction, avoid caffeine/alcohol, bladder training) is appropriate first-line management.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What does the presence of bladder trabeculation on cystoscopy indicate in a BPH patient?
options: A. Detrusor hypertrophy from chronic outlet obstruction
E. Normal variant in elderly men
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Trabeculation (thickened ridges of hypertrophied detrusor muscle) indicates the bladder has been working against chronic outlet obstruction. Advanced trabeculation may lead to saccule and diverticulum formation. Diverticula have no muscle layer and cannot contract, risking stasis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A patient with BPH develops bilateral hydronephrosis and creatinine of 320 μmol/L. What is the most important immediate management step?
options: A. Urethral catheterisation to decompress the bladder
B. CT urogram to exclude malignancy
E. Nephrology referral for dialysis planning
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: High-pressure chronic retention causing obstructive nephropathy requires urgent bladder decompression by catheterisation. This relieves back-pressure on kidneys. Creatinine typically improves significantly post-decompression. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: In the CombAT trial, what prostate volume threshold made combination therapy (dutasteride + tamsulosin) superior to monotherapy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: CombAT trial: combination therapy superior in men with prostate ≥30 mL and PSA ≥1.5 ng/mL, reducing risk of AUR and need for surgery. The 5-ARI reduces gland size (long-term benefit) while alpha blocker provides rapid symptomatic relief.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What is the pathological zone of the prostate affected in BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: BPH arises from hyperplasia of the transitional/periurethral zone (inner gland), which surrounds the urethra and enlarges to compress it. Prostate cancer typically arises from the peripheral zone (70%), detectable by DRE and biopsy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 69-year-old with BPH and angina is on doxazosin for LUTS. His cardiologist adds sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. What is the primary concern?
options: A. Severe hypotension from combined alpha blocker and PDE5 inhibitor
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Combination of alpha blockers and PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) causes significant additive hypotension due to vasodilation via different pathways. Contraindicated together or requires careful titration with time separation. Tamsulosin has slightly less interaction.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What is the PSA density threshold that raises concern for prostate cancer over BPH?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: PSA density (PSA ÷ prostate volume by TRUS) >0.15 ng/mL/cc suggests the PSA elevation is disproportionate to gland size, raising cancer suspicion. BPH elevates PSA proportionally to volume; cancer raises PSA independently of volume.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 78-year-old man develops a bladder stone on KUB X-ray. He has LUTS consistent with BPH. What is the most likely mechanism for stone formation?
options: A. Urinary stasis from incomplete bladder emptying
C. Recurrent UTI with urea-splitting organisms
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: BPH → incomplete bladder emptying → urinary stasis → concentrated urine → crystal nucleation and stone growth. Bladder stones in elderly men are strongly associated with BOO. Treatment requires both stone removal (cystolitholapaxy) and treatment of underlying BPH.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What percentage reduction in prostate volume can be expected after 6 months of finasteride therapy?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: 5-ARIs reduce prostate volume by 20-30% over 6 months by reducing DHT-driven glandular hyperplasia. This is a gradual effect unlike alpha blockers (rapid onset). Full symptomatic benefit may take 6-12 months.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What are the advantages of alfuzosin over tamsulosin in a man wishing to preserve ejaculatory function?
options: A. Alfuzosin causes less ejaculatory dysfunction than tamsulosin
B. Alfuzosin is more selective for alpha-1A receptors
C. Alfuzosin has faster onset of action
D. Alfuzosin does not cause postural hypotension
E. Alfuzosin has superior evidence for preventing urinary retention
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Tamsulosin (highly selective alpha-1A/D) causes retrograde ejaculation more frequently than alfuzosin. Alfuzosin's different receptor profile/pharmacokinetics results in less ejaculatory dysfunction. Important consideration in younger men with BPH.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 64-year-old is started on tamsulosin for BPH and reports dizziness on standing. What is the most appropriate action?
options: A. Advise taking at night after same-time meal and counsel on postural hypotension
B. Stop tamsulosin immediately and switch to finasteride
C. Reduce dose and add antihypertensive
D. Check lying and standing BP; if difference >20 mmHg discontinue permanently
E. Add fludrocortisone to prevent hypotension
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: First-dose and postural hypotension are known alpha blocker side effects. Taking tamsulosin at bedtime after the same meal each day minimises peak plasma levels during waking hours. Usually improves with continued use. Discontinuation not usually required.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What is the evidence for saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) in the treatment of BPH?
options: A. Large RCTs show no significant benefit over placebo
B. Equivalent efficacy to finasteride in all trials
C. Approved by NICE as first-line treatment
D. Reduces prostate volume by 15% at 12 months
E. Shown to prevent acute urinary retention
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: The STEP and CAMUS trials (NEJM 2006 and 2011) showed saw palmetto was no better than placebo for LUTS from BPH. Despite widespread use, it is not recommended in EAU/NICE guidelines due to lack of efficacy evidence.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A urodynamics report shows a detrusor pressure of 65 cmH2O with a Qmax of 7 mL/s. How should this be interpreted?
options: A. Bladder outlet obstruction (high pressure, low flow)
C. Underactive detrusor (low pressure, low flow)
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: High detrusor pressure (>40 cmH2O) with low Qmax (<10 mL/s) = bladder outlet obstruction on Abrams-Griffiths nomogram. This confirms BOO from BPH and predicts good surgical outcomes. Low pressure/low flow suggests detrusor failure, not obstruction.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What is the minimum voided volume required for a valid uroflowmetry result?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Uroflowmetry requires a voided volume of at least 150 mL (ideally 200-400 mL) for the result to be valid and reproducible. Voiding smaller volumes produces artificially low Qmax values unrelated to obstruction.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A 72-year-old with BPH on tamsulosin is scheduled for cataract surgery. What must be communicated to the ophthalmic surgeon?
options: A. Current or previous tamsulosin use — risk of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome
B. His BPH diagnosis and prostate size
D. His creatinine to assess renal function
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: IFIS (intraoperative floppy iris syndrome) is caused by alpha-1A blockade in iris dilator muscle. Even if tamsulosin has been stopped, IFIS risk persists. The ophthalmologist must be warned to use modified technique (pupil expansion devices, iris hooks, special viscoelastic agents).

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised complication of TURP?
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: TUR syndrome causes dilutional hyponatraemia (not hyperkalaemia) from hypotonic glycine irrigant absorption. Recognised TURP complications include retrograde ejaculation (most common), bleeding, urethral stricture, incontinence, bladder neck contracture, and TUR syndrome.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: An 80-year-old man with multiple comorbidities has an IPSS of 15 but no complications of BPH. He is reluctant to take medications. What non-pharmacological option is appropriate?
options: A. Watchful waiting with lifestyle modification and regular review
B. Immediate TURP as first line for moderate LUTS
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Watchful waiting is appropriate for moderate LUTS without complications, especially in men who are reluctant to take medication. Lifestyle advice includes fluid management, avoiding caffeine/alcohol, double voiding, and bladder training. Annual IPSS/flow rate/PVR review.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: What is the advantage of HoLEP over open simple prostatectomy for large BPH?
options: A. Less blood loss, shorter hospital stay, equivalent functional outcomes
B. Lower risk of retrograde ejaculation
C. Can be done under local anaesthesia
D. Does not require general/spinal anaesthesia
E. Preserves the prostatic urethra entirely
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: HoLEP vs open prostatectomy: equivalent functional outcomes (flow rate, symptom improvement) but HoLEP has significantly less blood loss (no need for transfusion), shorter catheter time, shorter hospital stay, and quicker recovery. Disadvantage: steep learning curve.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: A man presents with severe suprapubic pain and inability to void. Bladder scan shows 850 mL. After catheterisation, 900 mL of urine is drained. Over the next 4 hours, urine output is 1800 mL. What is occurring?
options: B. Urinary tract infection causing polyuria
C. Diabetes insipidus triggered by catheterisation
E. Catheter malposition causing CSF leakage
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: Post-obstructive diuresis follows relief of chronic obstruction: osmotic diuresis (retained urea/solutes), tubular dysfunction (impaired concentrating ability), and natriuretic peptide release. Defined as urine output >200 mL/hour for 2+ hours. Manage with 50% IV fluid replacement.

conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.question: In BPH, which prostate zone is hyperplastic, and which zone is predominantly affected in prostate cancer?
options: A. BPH: transitional zone; Cancer: peripheral zone
B. BPH: peripheral zone; Cancer: transitional zone
C. BPH: central zone; Cancer: peripheral zone
D. Both originate in the peripheral zone
E. BPH: anterior stroma; Cancer: central zone
conditions__UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hy.explanation: BPH arises from the transitional/periurethral zone (inner gland), compressing the urethra. Prostate adenocarcinoma arises predominantly from the peripheral zone (70%), which is palpable on DRE and accessible to systematic biopsy. Central zone cancers (5-10%) are typically aggressive.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: mpMRI is first-line investigation for suspected localised prostate cancer.
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 70-year-old man has an irregular hard prostate on DRE and PSA of 45. Most appropriate next investigation?

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Prostate cancer bone mets are osteoblastic (sclerotic). Myeloma/breast/lung = lytic.
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Bone metastases from prostate cancer on X-ray appear:

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: GnRH agonist initially ↑testosterone (tumour flare) — anti-androgen prevents this.
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A patient starts goserelin (GnRH agonist) for prostate cancer. What must be co-prescribed initially?

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Most elevated PSAs = BPH/prostatitis/infection. High false-positive rate.
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Prostate cancer PSA screening has which major limitation?
A prostate biopsy report states: primary Gleason pattern 4, secondary Gleason pattern 3. What is the correct ISUP grade group?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Gleason 4+3=7 corresponds to ISUP Grade Group 3. Gleason 3+4=7 is Grade Group 2. The distinction matters as 4+3 has worse prognosis than 3+4 despite same sum.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which Gleason score corresponds to ISUP Grade Group 1 and is generally managed with active surveillance in low-risk patients?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: ISUP Grade Group 1 = Gleason ≤6 (3+3). This is the lowest grade and, in low-risk patients (PSA <10, T1-T2a), active surveillance is appropriate to avoid overtreatment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 65-year-old man has PSA 7.2, Gleason 3+3=6, T2a on MRI, and 2/12 biopsy cores positive. What is the most appropriate management?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: This patient meets criteria for active surveillance: PSA <10, Gleason 6 (ISUP 1), T2a, ≤50% cores positive. Active surveillance avoids overtreatment and monitors with PSA 3-6 monthly and repeat MRI/biopsy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: What is the minimum PSA level that defines biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy?
options: A. ≥0.2 ng/mL on two consecutive tests
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: BCR after RP = PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL confirmed on two occasions. After EBRT, BCR = nadir + 2 ng/mL (Phoenix definition). Distinguishing is important for guiding salvage therapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A patient on long-term GnRH agonist therapy for prostate cancer develops back pain and decreased bone density on DEXA scan. Which drug is most appropriate to reduce fracture risk?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Denosumab (RANK-L inhibitor) is approved for preventing bone loss and fractures in men on ADT. It is also used to prevent skeletal-related events in bone-metastatic CRPC. Bisphosphonates are an alternative.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: What is the mechanism of action of abiraterone acetate in prostate cancer?
options: A. CYP17A1 inhibitor blocking androgen synthesis
C. GnRH agonist causing testosterone suppression
D. PARP inhibitor causing DNA damage
E. Microtubule stabiliser inhibiting cell division
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Abiraterone inhibits CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase), blocking androgen synthesis in the testes, adrenal glands and within the tumour itself. It must be combined with prednisolone to prevent mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalaemia).

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 72-year-old man with mCRPC and known BRCA2 mutation has progressed on enzalutamide. Which targeted therapy is most appropriate?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Olaparib is approved for mCRPC with BRCA1/2 or ATM mutations after prior enzalutamide or abiraterone. BRCA2 causes homologous recombination deficiency; PARP inhibition causes synthetic lethality in these tumours.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: In the ISUP grading system, which grade group has the worst prognosis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: ISUP Grade Group 5 (Gleason 9-10) has the worst prognosis with highest risk of biochemical recurrence, metastasis and cancer-specific mortality. Grade groups 1-5 represent a validated prognostic stratification improving on the original Gleason system.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: What is the key difference between HDR and LDR brachytherapy for prostate cancer?
options: A. HDR uses temporary Ir-192 wires; LDR uses permanent I-125 seeds
B. HDR is for high-risk disease only; LDR is for metastatic disease
C. LDR requires general anaesthesia; HDR does not
D. HDR uses external radiation; LDR uses internal seeds
E. LDR requires combination with ADT; HDR does not
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: LDR brachytherapy uses permanently implanted I-125 seeds delivering continuous low-dose radiation over months, suitable for low-intermediate risk. HDR uses temporary Ir-192 wires delivering short high-dose fractions, often combined with EBRT for higher-risk disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 68-year-old man with prostate cancer develops sudden onset leg weakness, urinary retention and constipation. What is the most important immediate step?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: This is metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC). High-dose dexamethasone must be given immediately to reduce cord oedema. Urgent MRI spine should follow. Radiotherapy within 24h if not a surgical candidate. Delay worsens neurological outcome.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which prostate zone is the origin of the majority (~70-80%) of prostate cancers?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: ~70-80% of prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which is the largest zone (70% of glandular tissue) and is palpable on DRE. The transitional zone is the site of BPH and ~20% of cancers, often found incidentally on TURP.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: What is T3b prostate cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: T3b = tumour invades seminal vesicle(s). T3a = extracapsular extension without SV invasion. T4 = invasion of adjacent structures (bladder, rectum, sphincter, levator muscles). This distinction guides surgical planning and adjuvant therapy decisions.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A patient develops hot flushes, gynaecomastia and fatigue 3 months after starting GnRH agonist therapy. These are typical side effects of which treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: ADT (GnRH agonists/antagonists) causes castrate testosterone levels → hot flushes (up to 80%), gynaecomastia, fatigue, loss of libido, erectile dysfunction, osteoporosis, and metabolic syndrome. Hot flushes can be treated with cyproterone acetate or SSRIs.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for detecting biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy at PSA levels <1 ng/mL?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: PSMA PET-CT is highly sensitive at low PSA levels (detects recurrence at PSA <0.5 ng/mL in many cases), far superior to conventional CT or bone scan. It identifies the site of recurrence to guide salvage radiotherapy targeting.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Locally advanced prostate cancer (T3-T4 N0 M0) is best managed with which combination?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: NICE/EAU guidelines recommend EBRT + long-term ADT (2-3 years) for locally advanced PCa. The combination significantly improves survival over either alone. High-risk patients may also benefit from addition of abiraterone or docetaxel.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 60-year-old man undergoes nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy. What is the primary purpose of preserving the neurovascular bundles?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: The neurovascular bundles (NVBs) run postero-laterally to the prostate and contain cavernous nerves controlling erectile function. Nerve-sparing surgery preserves these to reduce erectile dysfunction, though continence is primarily dependent on external urethral sphincter preservation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: PSA doubling time (PSADT) of less than 3 months after radical prostatectomy suggests which clinical situation?
options: A. Aggressive metastatic disease with poor prognosis
B. Localised recurrence suitable for salvage radiotherapy
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: PSADT <3 months indicates rapid PCa growth, suggesting metastatic disease with poor prognosis. PSADT >12 months is more likely to represent localised pelvic recurrence and responds better to salvage radiotherapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which gene mutation is associated with an 8-fold increased risk of prostate cancer and warrants consideration of PARP inhibitor therapy in mCRPC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: BRCA2 confers ~8-fold increased PCa risk (BRCA1 ~2-fold). BRCA2-mutated mCRPC is eligible for olaparib after prior enzalutamide/abiraterone. Germline testing is recommended for all metastatic PCa and high-risk localised disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 70-year-old man on long-term ADT for prostate cancer presents with confusion, constipation, polyuria and vomiting. Calcium is 3.2 mmol/L. What is the first-line treatment?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% saline is the immediate first step in hypercalcaemia (rehydration corrects 50% of cases). Once rehydrated, add IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) or denosumab. Furosemide is no longer routinely used. Treat underlying cause.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: What is the mechanism of action of enzalutamide compared to older anti-androgens like bicalutamide?
options: A. Blocks AR binding, nuclear translocation AND DNA binding
B. Only blocks AR ligand binding domain
C. Inhibits GnRH receptor in pituitary
E. Directly kills PCa cells by apoptosis
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Enzalutamide is a second-generation AR antagonist blocking multiple steps: androgen binding, AR nuclear translocation, and AR-DNA binding/co-activator recruitment. Bicalutamide only blocks ligand binding and can act as partial agonist in CRPC, making enzalutamide much more effective.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 67-year-old develops new bone pain and PSA rising to 180 ng/mL. Bone scan shows multiple sclerotic lesions. He is started on systemic therapy. What additional drug should be given to prevent skeletal-related events?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Zoledronic acid (IV bisphosphonate) or denosumab (RANK-L inhibitor) reduce skeletal-related events (SREs: fractures, spinal cord compression, need for surgery/radiotherapy) in bone-metastatic CRPC. Both require dental review before starting due to ONJ risk.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Salvage radiotherapy to the prostate bed is most effective in which scenario after radical prostatectomy?
options: A. Early BCR with PSA <0.5 ng/mL and PSADT >12 months
B. PSA >10 ng/mL with confirmed bone metastases
C. BCR with PSADT <3 months suggesting metastatic disease
D. BCR with positive lymph nodes on PSMA PET
E. BCR in a patient with Gleason 6 cancer
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Salvage RT is most effective when initiated early at low PSA (<0.5 ng/mL), with slow PSADT suggesting localised pelvic recurrence. PSADT <3 months and distant metastases on PSMA PET suggest systemic disease where RT alone is insufficient.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Lynch syndrome-associated prostate cancer is characterised by which molecular feature relevant to immunotherapy selection?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair deficiency) causes MSI-H tumours. Pembrolizumab (anti-PD1) is approved for all MSI-H/dMMR solid tumours regardless of site, including prostate cancer. Testing for MSI/MMR should be performed in all metastatic PCa patients.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Lutetium-177 PSMA therapy requires which prerequisite imaging before treatment?
options: A. PSMA PET-CT showing PSMA-positive disease
B. Bone scan showing >5 bone metastases
C. FDG PET-CT showing FDG-avid disease
D. MRI spine showing no cord compression
E. CT chest showing no pulmonary metastases
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Lu-177 PSMA therapy (VISION trial) requires PSMA PET-CT confirmation of PSMA-expressing disease. Patients with PSMA-negative lesions (especially FDG+/PSMA- discordance) are unlikely to respond. It is approved for mCRPC after taxane and AR pathway inhibitor.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A patient's prostate biopsy shows primary pattern 4 in 60% and secondary pattern 4 in 40%. What is the Gleason score and ISUP grade group?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: When both patterns are the same (4+4), the Gleason score is 8 = ISUP Grade Group 4. This carries a significantly worse prognosis than Gleason 7 and warrants definitive treatment rather than surveillance.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which side effect of abiraterone is prevented by co-prescribing prednisolone?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Abiraterone blocks CYP17A1, causing upstream ACTH elevation and accumulation of mineralocorticoid precursors (deoxycorticosterone, corticosterone) → hypertension, hypokalaemia, fluid retention. Prednisolone suppresses ACTH and provides glucocorticoid replacement.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which first-line systemic treatment combination is recommended for high-volume metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC)?
options: A. ADT + docetaxel or ADT + enzalutamide/abiraterone
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Intensification of ADT with docetaxel (CHAARTED/STAMPEDE), abiraterone (LATITUDE/STAMPEDE), enzalutamide (ARCHES/ENZAMET), or apalutamide (TITAN) significantly improves overall survival in mHSPC. ADT alone is no longer the standard of care for high-volume/high-risk metastatic disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 62-year-old man undergoes robotic radical prostatectomy. At 6 months, he reports stress urinary incontinence. What anatomical structure's preservation during surgery most influences continence?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Post-prostatectomy continence depends primarily on external urethral sphincter (rhabdosphincter) function, which provides the main mechanism of continence after removal of the prostate. The internal sphincter (bladder neck) is removed with the prostate. Nerve-sparing preserves erectile function, not primarily continence.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: In prostate TNM staging, N1 disease refers to which finding?
options: A. Regional lymph node metastasis (obturator/iliac/presacral nodes)
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: N1 = metastasis in regional lymph nodes (obturator, internal/external iliac, presacral, periprostatic nodes). Para-aortic, inguinal and mediastinal nodes are M1a (non-regional distant lymph nodes). N1 disease is treated with intensified systemic therapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A bone scan is indicated in newly diagnosed prostate cancer in which scenario?
options: A. PSA >10 ng/mL or Gleason ≥8 or T3/T4 or bone symptoms
B. All newly diagnosed prostate cancers regardless of PSA
D. Only when patient has bone pain
E. Gleason 6 disease at any PSA
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: EAU/NICE guidelines recommend bone scan for: PSA >10, Gleason ≥8, T3-T4 or any bone symptoms. For low-risk disease (PSA <10, Gleason ≤6, T1-T2), bone scan yield is very low (<1%) and not indicated.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Docetaxel chemotherapy in mCRPC works by which mechanism?
options: A. Microtubule stabilisation inhibiting mitosis and AR nuclear transport
B. Alkylation of DNA causing strand breaks
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Docetaxel stabilises microtubules (prevents depolymerisation), blocking cell division at G2/M phase. Crucially in PCa, it also inhibits AR nuclear translocation (AR is transported on microtubules), providing dual anti-tumour activity beyond pure cytotoxicity.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which statement about LDR brachytherapy for prostate cancer is correct?
options: A. Permanent I-125 seeds deliver radiation over months and are suitable for low-intermediate risk disease
B. Seeds are removed after treatment is complete
C. It is the preferred treatment for T3b disease
D. It requires concurrent ADT for all patients
E. It uses Iridium-192 as the radioactive isotope
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: LDR brachytherapy uses permanently implanted I-125 (or Pd-103) seeds that emit low-energy radiation over ~6 months. It is appropriate for low-to-intermediate risk localised PCa. Contraindications include large prostate (>50cc), previous TURP, significant LUTS, and T3+ disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A patient with mCRPC on zoledronic acid develops jaw pain and exposed bone after a dental extraction. What complication has occurred?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ) is a serious complication of bisphosphonates and denosumab. Risk factors: dental extractions, poor oral hygiene, duration of therapy. Prevention: dental assessment before starting, avoid extractions during therapy. Treatment: conservative (antibiotics, mouthwash), rarely surgery.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Active surveillance monitoring typically includes which combination of investigations?
options: A. PSA every 3-6 months, annual DRE, repeat mpMRI at 12 months, and repeat biopsy (targeted and systematic)
B. PSA annually and bone scan every 2 years
C. PSA monthly and CT pelvis 6-monthly
D. mpMRI annually with no PSA monitoring
E. PSA every 3 months and PSMA PET annually
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: NICE active surveillance protocol: PSA 3-6 monthly for 2 years then 6-monthly, annual DRE, repeat mpMRI at 12 months, and systematic + targeted repeat biopsy at 12 months (and subsequently if concern). Reclassification to higher grade triggers consideration of active treatment.

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: A 55-year-old man with T2b Gleason 8 prostate cancer (ISUP Grade 4) is found to have Lynch syndrome (MSH2 mutation). Which additional systemic therapy may be considered if he develops metastatic castration-resistant disease?
options: A. Pembrolizumab (anti-PD1 immunotherapy) if MSI-H confirmed
C. Abiraterone is contraindicated in Lynch syndrome
D. Docetaxel is not effective in Lynch-associated PCa
E. Enzalutamide is preferred over all other agents
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: Lynch syndrome causes mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR)/MSI-H tumours. Pembrolizumab has pan-tumour approval for dMMR/MSI-H cancers. Testing for MMR/MSI status in all metastatic PCa is recommended as ~3-5% have MSI-H disease (not only Lynch syndrome-associated).

conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.question: Which metabolic complication of long-term ADT is most directly monitored with periodic DEXA scanning?
conditions__UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer.explanation: ADT-induced testosterone suppression causes bone mineral density loss (2-3% per year) → osteoporosis and increased fracture risk. DEXA scanning at baseline and 1-2 yearly monitors BMD. Threshold for treatment: T-score ≤-2.5 or FRAX score indicating high fracture risk.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Aromatic amines (dye industry) + painless haematuria = classic bladder cancer.
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 65-year-old retired dye factory worker presents with visible painless haematuria. Diagnosis?

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: High-risk non-muscle-invasive disease → BCG stimulates local immune attack on tumour cells.
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A patient has a T1 (non-muscle-invasive) bladder tumour. What treatment is offered after TURBT?

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: T2+ requires radical cystectomy. Neoadjuvant chemo improves survival.
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer (T2+) is treated with:

A 62-year-old smoker presents with painless frank haematuria. Flexible cystoscopy shows a 2 cm papillary tumour on the posterior wall. TURBT histology confirms pTa, low-grade TCC. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Single instillation of intravesical mitomycin C within 24 hours of TURBT
D. CT urogram and watchful waiting
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Low-risk NMIBC (pTa, LG, single tumour): single instillation of mitomycin C (or epirubicin) within 24 hours of TURBT reduces recurrence by ~12-15%. BCG is reserved for intermediate/high-risk NMIBC. Radical cystectomy not indicated for NMIBC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the bladder is classified as which T stage?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: CIS = Tis (tumour in situ): flat high-grade intraepithelial carcinoma confined to urothelium. Despite being 'non-invasive', CIS is biologically aggressive with 50% progression to MIBC without treatment. Requires BCG immunotherapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 55-year-old man who worked for 20 years as a rubber industry worker presents with haematuria. What occupational carcinogen is implicated?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Aromatic amines (beta-naphthylamine, benzidine) are the key occupational carcinogens for bladder TCC, found in rubber, dye, textile, and leather industries. Latency period 15-40 years. Recognised as industrial disease. Smoking is the single biggest risk factor overall.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 70-year-old man is found to have T2 bladder cancer. What does T2 staging mean?
options: A. Tumour invades muscularis propria (detrusor muscle)
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: T2 = muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), invading the muscularis propria/detrusor. T2a = inner half, T2b = outer half. This is a critical staging boundary — T2+ requires radical intent treatment (cystectomy or radiotherapy ± chemo). T1 invades lamina propria only.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the sensitivity of urine cytology for high-grade TCC vs low-grade TCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Urine cytology is highly sensitive for high-grade TCC and CIS (70-90%) because these cells are poorly differentiated and exfoliate readily. Low-grade tumours have cells that appear near-normal, making cytology unreliable (<50% sensitivity). Never use cytology alone to exclude malignancy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 45-year-old Egyptian man presents with haematuria and obstructive voiding. Cystoscopy shows a mass near the trigone, and biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most likely aetiology?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Schistosoma haematobium (bilharzia) is endemic in Egypt/sub-Saharan Africa and is the classic cause of SCC of the bladder. Chronic egg deposition causes sustained inflammation → squamous metaplasia → SCC. TCC is more common in Western countries where smoking predominates.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A patient with T1 high-grade bladder cancer undergoes TURBT + BCG. Three months later, repeat cystoscopy shows persistent CIS despite 2 BCG courses. What is the next appropriate management?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: BCG-refractory NMIBC (failure to respond after adequate BCG — 2 induction courses at minimum) in high-risk disease (T1HG, CIS) has a high progression risk. Radical cystectomy is the recommended treatment. Delay increases risk of progression to MIBC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is blue light cystoscopy (photodynamic diagnosis) and what agent is used?
options: A. Hexaminolevulinate instilled intravesically; tumours fluoresce pink/red under blue light
B. Methylene blue IV injection; lymph nodes identified under UV light
C. Narrow-band imaging with no intravesical agent required
D. 5-aminolevulinic acid systemic injection; bladder assessed at laparoscopy
E. Fluorescein intravesical instillation for ureteric identification
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: PDD (hexaminolevulinate/HAL) is instilled intravesically 1-2 hours before TURBT. HAL is metabolised to fluorescent porphyrins in tumour cells, which appear pink/red under blue (380 nm) light. Detects ~25% more CIS and flat lesions than white light, reducing recurrence.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 68-year-old woman undergoes radical cystectomy for T2 bladder cancer. The surgeon creates an ileal conduit. What complication is specific to this urinary diversion?
options: A. Stomal stenosis and parastomal hernia
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Ileal conduit (Bricker diversion) specific complications: stomal stenosis, parastomal hernia, stoma retraction, uretero-ileal anastomotic stricture, urinary infection, metabolic acidosis (ileal absorption of urine), and vitamin B12 deficiency (ileal segment loss).

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: Which chemotherapy regimen is now preferred over MVAC as first-line treatment for metastatic urothelial carcinoma?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: GC (Gemcitabine + Cisplatin) has equivalent overall survival to MVAC (~13-14 months) with significantly less toxicity. GC causes less grade 3/4 neutropenia, mucositis, alopecia, and treatment-related deaths. It is now the standard first-line chemotherapy for metastatic urothelial carcinoma.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 65-year-old with T3 bladder cancer on CT scan has hydronephrosis on the right. What does this suggest?
options: A. Ureteric involvement at the trigone indicating locally advanced disease
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Hydronephrosis in bladder cancer indicates ureteric obstruction, typically from a trigonal/lateral wall tumour or from perivesical extension. It suggests locally advanced disease, is an adverse prognostic factor, and may influence surgical planning (ureteric reimplantation at cystectomy).

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the NICE 2-week wait criteria for bladder cancer referral?
options: A. Aged ≥45 with unexplained visible haematuria, or aged ≥60 with unexplained non-visible haematuria + dysuria or a raised WCC
B. Only patients >50 with haematuria and weight loss
C. Only patients with haematuria + positive urine cytology
D. Haematuria in patients with occupational risk factors only
E. Recurrent haematuria >3 episodes in 12 months
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.answer: A. Aged ≥45 with unexplained visible haematuria, or aged ≥60 with unexplained non-visible haematuria + dysuria or a raised WCC
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: NICE NG12: urgent 2-week-wait referral for adults aged ≥45 with unexplained visible haematuria (or visible haematuria persisting/recurring after treatment of a UTI), and adults aged ≥60 with unexplained non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or a raised white-cell count.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A patient has a positive urine cytology but normal flexible cystoscopy findings. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: A. CT urogram to image upper tracts for TCC
C. Bladder biopsy under GA immediately
D. Discharge as cystoscopy is normal
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Positive cytology with normal cystoscopy may indicate upper tract TCC (renal pelvis/ureter) or CIS not visible on standard white light cystoscopy. CT urogram images the entire urothelium. Consider blue light cystoscopy/selective upper tract washings if CT negative.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 58-year-old with T2N0M0 bladder cancer who is unfit for surgery due to severe COPD. What is the preferred bladder-preserving treatment?
options: A. Trimodal therapy: maximal TURBT + concurrent chemoradiotherapy
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Trimodal bladder preservation for MIBC: maximal TURBT (to reduce tumour burden) + concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin as radiosensitiser + external beam RT). Achieved comparable OS to cystectomy in selected patients. Requires complete TURBT and regular surveillance cystoscopy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What percentage of bladder cancers in Western countries are transitional cell carcinoma (TCC/urothelial carcinoma)?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: TCC (urothelial carcinoma) accounts for ~90% of bladder cancers in Western countries. SCC accounts for ~5% (associated with chronic irritation, Schistosoma), adenocarcinoma ~1-2% (urachal or metaplastic). In Schistosoma-endemic regions, SCC may represent up to 80%.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 72-year-old man has BCG instillation. Two days later he develops fever of 39.5°C, rigors, and hypotension. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
options: A. BCG sepsis; treat with anti-tuberculosis drugs (isoniazid + rifampicin ± ethambutol)
B. Bacterial UTI; treat with ciprofloxacin
C. BCG cystitis; treat with pyridoxine and NSAIDs
D. Septicaemia from bladder perforation; emergency laparotomy
E. Drug reaction; stop BCG and give antihistamines
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: BCG sepsis (systemic BCG infection) is rare but life-threatening, occurring after intravesical BCG. Presents with high fever, rigors, hepatitis, pneumonitis. Treat with anti-TB drugs (isoniazid + rifampicin, ± ethambutol) for 6 months. Corticosteroids added for severe cases. Discontinue BCG permanently.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the contraindication to post-TURBT single instillation of intravesical mitomycin C?
options: A. Suspected bladder perforation during TURBT
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Single instillation mitomycin C is contraindicated if bladder perforation occurred during TURBT — systemic absorption would cause severe toxicity (bone marrow suppression, systemic mitomycin C toxicity). Also contraindicated in frank haematuria and known hypersensitivity.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 67-year-old woman undergoes radical cystectomy and neobladder construction. What is the major long-term functional concern with a neobladder?
options: A. Urinary retention requiring clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CIC)
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Neobladder (orthotopic ileal reservoir): constructed from ileum anastomosed to urethra. Patients void by Valsalva/abdominal straining. Up to 20-40% develop daytime incontinence and up to 70% have nocturnal incontinence initially. Urinary retention requiring CIC affects ~20-25%. Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis can occur (ileal segment absorbs urine).

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What staging investigation is essential before deciding between radical cystectomy and bladder preservation for MIBC?
options: A. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (staging CT) + MRI pelvis
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: CT CAP (staging CT) assesses nodal/metastatic disease. MRI pelvis provides better soft tissue detail for local staging (depth of invasion, extravesical extension, lymph nodes). EUA with bimanual examination assesses tumour fixation. Both needed for treatment planning in MIBC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: Pembrolizumab is licensed for bladder cancer in which specific setting?
options: A. Metastatic urothelial carcinoma after platinum-based chemotherapy
C. Adjunct to BCG for CIS
D. Post-cystectomy adjuvant therapy in all patients
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) is licensed as second-line treatment for advanced/metastatic urothelial carcinoma progressing after or on platinum-based chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-045). It is also used in first-line cisplatin-ineligible patients with PD-L1 positive tumours and BCG-unresponsive NMIBC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 50-year-old with upper tract TCC in the right renal pelvis undergoes nephroureterectomy. What follow-up is essential?
options: A. Cystoscopy surveillance every 3 months for 2 years (high risk of bladder recurrence)
C. No follow-up required as curative resection performed
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: After nephroureterectomy for upper tract TCC, ~30-40% develop metachronous bladder tumours (urothelial field change). Bladder cystoscopy every 3 months for 2 years is mandatory. CT urogram assesses contralateral upper tract. Bladder instillation post-operatively is under investigation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 68-year-old is referred urgently with painless visible haematuria. He is a lifelong non-smoker. What other risk factor should be specifically asked about?
options: A. Occupational exposure (rubber, dye, leather, printing industries)
C. Family history of renal cell carcinoma
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines (beta-naphthylamine, benzidine) in rubber, dye, textile, leather, and printing industries is the second most important risk factor for TCC after smoking. Latency 15-40 years. Prescribed industrial disease in UK — important medicolegal implications.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the difference between flexible and rigid cystoscopy in bladder cancer management?
options: A. Flexible: diagnostic/surveillance (outpatient, no anaesthesia); Rigid: therapeutic TURBT (theatre, GA/spinal)
B. Flexible: better visualisation; Rigid: used only for women
C. Flexible: for CIS diagnosis; Rigid: for papillary tumours only
D. Both identical in diagnostic yield
E. Flexible: performed under GA; Rigid: local anaesthesia
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Flexible cystoscopy: diagnostic, outpatient, local anaesthetic gel, good patient tolerance — used for initial haematuria investigation and surveillance. Rigid cystoscopy: under GA/spinal, allows operative intervention (TURBT), bimanual EUA, random biopsies, and fulguration. Blue light requires rigid cystoscope.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 63-year-old with NMIBC (pT1HG) has a repeat TURBT 6 weeks after initial resection. Why is repeat TURBT recommended for T1HG disease?
options: A. Up to 50% have residual tumour and 10% are upstaged to T2 on repeat resection
B. To administer intravesical BCG under the same anaesthetic
C. To perform random biopsies for CIS surveillance only
D. Routine protocol for all TURBT regardless of grade/stage
E. To confirm biopsy margins before BCG therapy
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Repeat TURBT 4-6 weeks after initial resection is recommended for T1HG disease (EAU guidelines) because: ~50% have residual tumour, ~10% are upstaged to T2 (muscle-invasive) changing management to cystectomy. Essential before starting BCG to ensure accurate staging.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What are the 5-year survival rates for muscle-invasive (T2) vs metastatic bladder cancer?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: 5-year survival: Ta/T1 ~80-90%, T2 organ-confined ~50-60%, T3 perivesical fat ~30-40%, T4 adjacent organ invasion ~10-20%, M1 metastatic <10%. Lymph node status significantly impacts prognosis — node-positive N1 ~20-30% 5-year OS.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 30-year-old female presents with haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Urinary tract infection or renal calculus
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: In young patients (<40), haematuria is most commonly caused by UTI, renal/ureteric calculi, IgA nephropathy, or exercise-related haematuria. Bladder cancer is rare under 40. However, persistent or recurrent visible haematuria requires investigation regardless of age. Young women with haematuria should have MSU first.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What metabolic complication can occur following urinary diversion using an ileal conduit?
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Ileal conduit: the ileal mucosa absorbs NH4+ and Cl- from urine and secretes HCO3-, causing a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis (plus a risk of B12 deficiency if the terminal ileum is used). Colonic diversions (e.g. ureterosigmoidostomy) cause the same hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis by the same mechanism.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 74-year-old has a T4a bladder cancer invading the prostate. What does T4a signify?
options: A. Tumour invades prostate stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus, or vagina
B. Tumour invades pelvic sidewall or abdominal wall
C. Tumour invades perivesical fat microscopically
D. Tumour invades perivesical fat macroscopically
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: T4a: tumour invades prostate stroma, seminal vesicles (in men), or uterus/vagina (in women) — adjacent pelvic organs. T4b: tumour invades pelvic sidewall or abdominal wall. T4b disease is generally inoperable; T4a may still be resectable with radical cystectomy and extended resection.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the role of neoadjuvant chemotherapy before radical cystectomy for T2 bladder cancer?
options: A. Cisplatin-based NAC improves 5-year OS by ~5-8% and is recommended if cisplatin-eligible
B. It is contraindicated before cystectomy as it delays surgery
C. It is equivalent to adjuvant chemotherapy post-cystectomy
D. Only indicated if nodal involvement confirmed on CT
E. Carboplatin-based NAC is preferred over cisplatin
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Level 1A evidence (BA06, SWOG trials): cisplatin-based NAC (GC or MVAC) before radical cystectomy improves OS by 5-8% at 5 years. May downstage tumour — pT0 at cystectomy in ~30% cases. Ineligible if GFR <50 mL/min. Carboplatin is not an acceptable substitute for NAC in fit patients.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the surveillance protocol for high-risk NMIBC after BCG therapy?
options: A. Cystoscopy every 3 months for 2 years, then 6-monthly for life
C. CT urogram annually with no cystoscopy
D. Cystoscopy at 3 months then discharge if negative
E. Urine cytology every 6 months without cystoscopy
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: High-risk NMIBC (T1HG, CIS, multiple/large/recurrent): cystoscopy + cytology every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for lifetime (EAU guidelines). High risk of recurrence (50-70%) and progression (10-20% at 5 years). Annual CT urogram recommended for upper tract surveillance.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A patient with bladder cancer has a CT showing a 3 cm lymph node at the aortic bifurcation. What N stage is this?
options: A. N3 — common iliac lymph node involvement
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.answer: A. N3 — common iliac lymph node involvement
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: In bladder cancer TNM (8th ed.) the N-stage has no size criterion: N1 = a single node in the true pelvis, N2 = multiple true-pelvis nodes, N3 = common iliac node(s). A node at the aortic bifurcation is a common iliac node → N3. Nodes above this (para-aortic) are classed as M1a distant disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the mechanism by which BCG treats bladder cancer?
options: A. Stimulates innate and adaptive immune response via Toll-like receptors; induces cytokine release destroying tumour cells
B. Directly cytotoxic DNA alkylation like mitomycin C
C. Inhibits tumour angiogenesis via VEGF suppression
D. Induces apoptosis via p53 pathway activation
E. Blocks PD-L1 on tumour cells
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: BCG (attenuated Mycobacterium bovis) binds fibronectin on urothelium → internalised by tumour cells → TLR activation → pro-inflammatory cytokine cascade (IL-2, IL-12, TNF-α, IFN-γ) → Th1-mediated immune response → tumour cell killing. The exact mechanism remains incompletely understood.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 60-year-old woman with painless haematuria is found on CT urogram to have a filling defect in the left renal pelvis. Urine cytology is positive. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: A. Upper tract TCC; nephroureterectomy (laparoscopic or open)
B. Renal cell carcinoma; partial nephrectomy
C. Bladder cancer with upper tract involvement; radical cystectomy
D. Renal calculus; ureteroscopy and stone fragmentation
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: Filling defect in renal pelvis + positive cytology = upper tract TCC. Gold standard treatment is nephroureterectomy (removing kidney, ureter, and bladder cuff). Laparoscopic approach preferred. Post-operative bladder surveillance mandatory given 30-40% risk of bladder TCC. Ureteroscopy + biopsy used for diagnosis in selected cases.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the WHO 2004 grading classification for non-invasive papillary urothelial tumours?
options: A. PUNLMP, low-grade urothelial carcinoma, high-grade urothelial carcinoma
B. G1, G2, G3 well/moderate/poorly differentiated
C. Low grade, intermediate grade, high grade
D. Ta, T1, CIS based on depth only
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: WHO 2004: PUNLMP (papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential — very low recurrence, almost zero progression), low-grade urothelial carcinoma (LG), high-grade urothelial carcinoma (HG). HG has high recurrence (~70%) and progression risk (~20%). Replaces old G1-G3 terminology.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: Which of the following is a contraindication to BCG intravesical therapy?
options: A. Active immunosuppression (e.g., post-renal transplant on azathioprine)
C. CIS confined to the bladder
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: BCG contraindications: immunosuppression (HIV, transplant immunosuppressants — risk of disseminated BCG infection), active TB, gross haematuria (systemic absorption risk), traumatic catheterisation, active UTI, recent TURBT (<2-3 weeks). Age alone is not a contraindication.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: A 66-year-old has T3bN1M0 urothelial carcinoma. He is cisplatin-eligible. What is the recommended treatment pathway?
options: A. Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy then radical cystectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy
B. Immediate radical cystectomy then adjuvant chemotherapy
D. BCG induction course then reassessment
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: T3N1 (locally advanced, node-positive but potentially resectable): cisplatin-eligible patients should receive NAC first (improves systemic disease control and OS) followed by radical cystectomy + extended pelvic lymphadenectomy. Adjuvant pembrolizumab may be offered post-cystectomy for high-risk pT3/T4 or node-positive disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.question: What is the significance of PD-L1 expression in bladder cancer treatment decisions?
options: A. PD-L1 positivity (CPS ≥10) predicts response to checkpoint inhibitors in cisplatin-ineligible first-line metastatic disease
B. PD-L1 negativity is required for BCG therapy
C. PD-L1 expression determines surgical resectability
D. PD-L1 testing is performed on urine cytology samples
E. PD-L1 positivity contraindicates platinum chemotherapy
conditions__UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer.explanation: PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) ≥10 on immunohistochemistry identifies patients likely to benefit from pembrolizumab or atezolizumab as first-line therapy when cisplatin is contraindicated. In cisplatin-fit patients, chemotherapy is still preferred regardless of PD-L1 status. PD-L1 testing guides second-line checkpoint inhibitor decisions.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Cannonball metastases = classic haematogenous spread of RCC to lungs.
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: CXR shows multiple well-defined circular opacities throughout both lung fields in a patient with haematuria. Diagnosis?

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: RCC can secrete EPO autonomously → secondary polycythaemia.
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A patient with RCC has raised Hb 19.5. This is due to:

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Left testicular vein → left renal vein. Tumour thrombus in left renal vein obstructs drainage.
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A left-sided varicocele that does not decompress on lying down should prompt investigation for:
A 58-year-old woman with a 6cm solid enhancing renal mass is found to have a normal contralateral kidney on CT. What is the most appropriate surgical approach?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: A 6cm renal mass (T1b/T2) with a normal contralateral kidney is best managed with radical nephrectomy. Partial nephrectomy is preferred for T1a tumours (<4cm) and imperative when the contralateral kidney is absent or dysfunctional. For T1b, partial can be attempted by experienced surgeons.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Clear cell RCC is associated with loss of which tumour suppressor gene located on chromosome 3p?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: VHL gene on chromosome 3p25 is mutated or silenced (by methylation) in ~80% of sporadic clear cell RCCs. VHL protein normally targets HIF-1α for ubiquitin-mediated degradation; loss leads to HIF accumulation and downstream VEGF/PDGF upregulation driving angiogenesis.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A 45-year-old man with multiple bilateral renal tumours, cutaneous fibrofolliculomas, and a history of spontaneous pneumothorax presents with a renal mass biopsy showing chromophobe RCC. Which hereditary syndrome is most likely?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (FLCN mutation) is characterised by: fibrofolliculomas (skin), pulmonary cysts/spontaneous pneumothorax, and renal tumours (chromophobe RCC, oncocytoma, hybrid). VHL causes clear cell RCC. HLRCC causes type 2 papillary RCC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: The IMDC prognostic score for metastatic RCC includes which six factors?
options: A. KPS <80%, time to systemic therapy <1yr, Hb below LLN, Ca above ULN, neutrophils above ULN, platelets above ULN
B. Age >65, tumour size >7cm, bilateral disease, LN involvement, bone mets, liver mets
C. ECOG >1, PSA >20, Gleason >7, T3+, N1, M1
D. GFR <60, haematuria, weight loss, night sweats, fever, anaemia
E. Smoking, obesity, hypertension, ADPKD, family history, prior nephrectomy
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: IMDC criteria (Heng criteria): KPS <80%, time from diagnosis to systemic therapy <1 year, haemoglobin below LLN, corrected calcium above ULN, neutrophils above ULN, platelets above ULN. 0 = favourable (median OS ~43 months); 1-2 = intermediate (~22 months); 3-6 = poor (~8 months).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A CT scan of a renal mass shows HU attenuation of -25 within the tumour. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Macroscopic fat within a renal mass (CT attenuation <-10 HU, typically -20 to -100 HU) is diagnostic of AML. RCC does not contain macroscopic fat. AML >4cm has significant haemorrhage risk and may need embolisation. Fat-poor AML can mimic RCC and may require biopsy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A 52-year-old woman with ADPKD is found on surveillance ultrasound to have a solid 3.5cm mass in her right kidney. What is the next appropriate step?
options: A. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast for characterisation and staging
B. Urgent nephrectomy without further imaging
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: ADPKD patients have 5-10 times increased RCC risk. A solid enhancing mass in an ADPKD kidney requires CT TAP for characterisation and staging before surgical planning. Nephrectomy may be required but staging must be performed first to exclude metastatic disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Which first-line treatment is recommended for intermediate/poor-risk metastatic clear cell RCC?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: CheckMate 214 established ipilimumab + nivolumab as superior to sunitinib in intermediate/poor-risk mRCC, with improved OS and higher complete response rate. Cabozantinib + nivolumab (CheckMate 9ER) and pembrolizumab + axitinib are also approved first-line options.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A renal cyst is classified as Bosniak III on CT. What does this indicate and what is the recommended management?
options: A. Thick irregular septa or calcification; ~54% malignancy risk; surgical resection recommended
B. Simple benign cyst; no follow-up needed
D. Solid enhancing components; >90% malignancy risk
E. Benign haemorrhagic cyst; annual follow-up
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Bosniak III = thick irregular septa, coarse/irregular calcification, heterogeneous; ~54% malignancy risk → surgical excision recommended. Bosniak I (0% malignancy, discharge), II (<1%), IIF (follow-up), III (~54%, excise), IV (>90%, excise).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A patient with T3b RCC has tumour thrombus extending below the diaphragm within the IVC. What is the surgical approach?
options: A. Radical nephrectomy with IVC thrombectomy without cardiopulmonary bypass
D. Radical nephrectomy with cardiopulmonary bypass
E. Embolisation of IVC thrombus followed by nephrectomy
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: T3b = infradiaphragmatic IVC thrombus; managed with radical nephrectomy + IVC thrombectomy without needing cardiopulmonary bypass. T3c = supradiaphragmatic or right atrial extension → requires cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. Outcomes remain acceptable with complete resection.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Which histological subtype of RCC is most strongly associated with cigarette smoking and accounts for approximately 75% of all renal cancers?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Clear cell RCC accounts for ~75% of RCCs and has the strongest association with smoking, obesity and VHL pathway alterations. Chromophobe and papillary subtypes have weaker smoking associations. Medullary RCC is associated with sickle cell trait/disease.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A 66-year-old man with metastatic RCC develops mouth ulcers and new pulmonary infiltrates while on second-line everolimus. Which side effect is most likely?
options: A. Everolimus-induced stomatitis and non-infectious pneumonitis
B. Metastatic spread to lungs and gingiva
D. Sunitinib toxicity (drug not being taken)
E. Immune-mediated toxicity from prior nivolumab
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor) commonly causes: stomatitis/aphthous ulcers (~40%), non-infectious pneumonitis (~14%), hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidaemia, immunosuppression and fatigue. Pneumonitis may require dose reduction or steroids. Distinguish from infection before steroid use.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: What is the most appropriate investigation for characterising a complex renal cyst in a patient with iodine contrast allergy and CKD stage 3?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: CEUS uses microbubble contrast agents which are not nephrotoxic and do not contain iodine — safe in CKD and contrast allergy. It provides real-time assessment of vascularity/enhancement in renal cysts and is incorporated into Bosniak classification (2019 update). MRI with gadolinium is an alternative.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with multiple uterine fibroids requiring hysterectomy and cutaneous leiomyomas. Genetic testing reveals FH (fumarate hydratase) mutation. What renal cancer surveillance is indicated?
options: A. Annual MRI abdomen from age 8-10 (or at diagnosis) due to HLRCC-associated aggressive papillary type 2 RCC
B. No renal surveillance needed as FH mutation only affects smooth muscle
D. CT chest/abdomen every 2 years from age 50
E. Renal biopsy at diagnosis then 5-yearly surveillance
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: HLRCC (Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and RCC, FH mutation) is associated with highly aggressive type 2 papillary RCC that can metastasise even at very small sizes. Annual MRI surveillance should begin early (age 8-10). Unlike VHL-related RCC where watchful waiting of small tumours is safe, HLRCC-associated RCC requires prompt treatment even when small.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: In TNM staging for RCC, T1a refers to which tumour size?
options: E. Any size with renal vein invasion
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: RCC T-staging by size: T1a ≤4cm, T1b 4-7cm, T2a 7-10cm, T2b >10cm (all confined to kidney). T3 = extracapsular extension regardless of size. T1a is important as it typically qualifies for partial nephrectomy or ablative therapy.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Sunitinib inhibits which molecular targets in RCC?
options: A. VEGFR1/2/3, PDGFR-α/β, c-KIT, FLT3, RET
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Sunitinib is a multi-TKI targeting VEGFR1/2/3 (anti-angiogenic), PDGFR-α/β, c-KIT, FLT3 and RET. This broad kinase inhibition accounts for its activity and also its toxicity profile: hypertension, hand-foot syndrome, thyroid dysfunction, fatigue, mucositis, cardiotoxicity.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A 70-year-old man with a 2.5cm solid renal mass is unfit for surgery due to severe COPD and heart failure. What is the best minimally invasive treatment option?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: For patients unfit for surgery with small renal masses (<3-4cm), thermal ablation (RFA or cryoablation) offers acceptable oncological outcomes with low morbidity. RFA uses heat (90-100°C), cryoablation uses freezing. Local recurrence ~5-10% vs <3% for surgery. SBRT (stereotactic body RT) is an emerging alternative.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Cabozantinib has superior efficacy to sunitinib in intermediate/poor-risk mRCC partly because it targets which additional pathways beyond VEGFR that drive resistance?
options: B. PARP and DNA repair pathways
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Cabozantinib targets VEGFR2 + MET + AXL. MET and AXL are upregulated as resistance mechanisms to VEGFR-only inhibition (sunitinib/pazopanib). The CABOSUN trial showed cabozantinib superior PFS vs sunitinib in intermediate/poor-risk patients; METEOR trial showed superiority vs everolimus in second-line.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: How does RCC cause a left-sided varicocele?
options: A. Left renal vein tumour thrombus obstructs left testicular vein drainage
B. Retroperitoneal lymph node metastases compress the vas deferens
C. Paraneoplastic testosterone excess causes varicocele
D. Direct invasion of testicular vessels by RCC
E. Right-sided RCC causes bilateral varicocele via IVC obstruction
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein (at right angles). Left-sided RCC with renal vein tumour thrombus obstructs this drainage → venous hypertension → left varicocele. Right testicular vein drains directly into IVC, so right-sided RCC rarely causes varicocele. New adult left varicocele warrants renal imaging.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Stauffer syndrome is a paraneoplastic manifestation of RCC causing which liver abnormality?
options: A. Non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction (elevated LFTs, hepatosplenomegaly) reversible after nephrectomy
C. Budd-Chiari syndrome from IVC thrombus
D. Autoimmune hepatitis triggered by tumour antigens
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Stauffer syndrome = paraneoplastic hepatic dysfunction without hepatic metastases; elevated ALP, AST, ALT, bilirubin, prolonged PT; hepatosplenomegaly; caused by cytokine-mediated (IL-6) effect on liver. Resolves after nephrectomy if no mets; recurrence suggests relapse. Important to distinguish from true hepatic mets.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Which statement about partial nephrectomy (PN) versus radical nephrectomy (RN) is correct for T1a RCC?
options: A. PN is preferred as it preserves renal function with equivalent oncological outcomes
B. RN is always preferred as it has lower recurrence rates
C. PN should only be used in solitary kidney situations
D. RN is preferred for posterior tumours
E. Both approaches have equivalent impact on long-term renal function
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: For T1a RCC (<4cm), partial nephrectomy is the standard of care where technically feasible, providing equivalent cancer-specific survival with preservation of nephrons → better long-term eGFR → reduced cardiovascular mortality. The absolute imperative for PN: solitary kidney, bilateral tumours, pre-existing CKD, hereditary RCC.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A patient with metastatic RCC achieves good disease control on sunitinib for 18 months then progresses. What is the most appropriate next-line treatment according to current guidelines?
options: C. Restart sunitinib at higher dose
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: After first-line VEGFR TKI failure, second-line options with OS benefit include cabozantinib (METEOR trial) and nivolumab (CheckMate 025). Nivolumab showed OS benefit over everolimus. Everolimus is no longer considered the preferred second-line option given availability of these agents.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A CT scan of a 55-year-old man reveals a 4.5cm right renal mass with central stellate scar and homogeneous enhancement. Biopsy shows large cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and numerous mitochondria on electron microscopy. What is the diagnosis?
options: E. Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Oncocytoma: benign tumour; cells packed with mitochondria giving eosinophilic granular cytoplasm; central stellate scar on CT (not pathognomonic but suggestive); cannot be reliably distinguished from chromophobe RCC pre-operatively; nephrectomy is curative and diagnostic. No malignant transformation.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Erythropoietin (EPO) production causing paraneoplastic polycythaemia in RCC results from which pathway?
options: A. VHL loss → HIF accumulation → EPO gene transcription
B. Autonomous EPO secretion by the tumour unrelated to VHL
C. Renal vein compression causing renal ischaemia → EPO release
D. PTHrP secretion stimulating bone marrow erythropoiesis
E. Direct invasion of bone marrow by RCC
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: VHL loss in clear cell RCC → HIF-1α/HIF-2α stabilisation → HIF-2α specifically drives EPO gene transcription → autonomous EPO production → erythrocytosis/polycythaemia. This is the same mechanism that causes high-altitude polycythaemia (physiological HIF activation).

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: In Robson staging of RCC, which stage indicates involvement of the renal vein or inferior vena cava?
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Robson Stage III = renal vein or IVC involvement, OR regional lymph node metastases. Stage I = confined to kidney; Stage II = within Gerota fascia; Stage IV = adjacent organ invasion (IVa) or distant metastases (IVb). TNM staging has largely replaced Robson in modern practice.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: A 48-year-old woman is found to have a 1.5cm incidental renal mass on CT for unrelated abdominal pain. CT report describes homogeneous enhancement without fat. What is the most appropriate management?
options: A. CT or MRI at 6-12 months for surveillance of likely benign lesion
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: Small incidentally found renal masses (<2cm) have a significant rate of benignity (~30%). EAU guidelines recommend active surveillance with CT/MRI at 6-12 months for small solid masses. Biopsy can guide management. For masses <1cm, initial surveillance is most appropriate.

conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.question: Pazopanib is preferred over sunitinib in some patients due to its more favourable side effect profile. Which side effects are more common with sunitinib than pazopanib?
options: B. Hepatotoxicity and hair colour change
E. Osteonecrosis of jaw and hypocalcaemia
conditions__UROLOGY__Renal Cell Carcinom.explanation: COMPARZ trial showed sunitinib causes more fatigue, hand-foot syndrome, and thrombocytopenia; pazopanib causes more hepatotoxicity, hair depigmentation and weight loss. Oncological outcomes (PFS/OS) were similar. Patient preference studies (PISCES trial) showed preference for pazopanib QoL profile.
